## 第641篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

In many countries the number of overweight children and teenagers has risen sharply in recent decades. What are the causes of this trend, and what measures could be taken to reverse it?

### 文章

Rates of obesity among children and adolescents have climbed steeply in a great many countries over the last thirty years. The causes lie in the way modern food and modern childhood have changed together, and the remedies will have to change both.

The first cause is the economics of eating. Processed food engineered to be high in sugar, fat and salt is now the cheapest way to feed a family quickly, and it is marketed hardest at exactly the age group least equipped to resist it. A parent finishing a shift at seven in the evening is not choosing between a home-cooked meal and a takeaway on equal terms; one costs an hour they do not have. The second cause is the disappearance of incidental movement. Children who once walked to school and played unsupervised in the street are now driven and screened, so the exercise that used to happen without anybody planning it has to be deliberately scheduled instead.

Two measures follow from this. Governments could use tax and regulation to change the relative price of what is on the shelf — a levy on sugary drinks, restrictions on advertising aimed at children — so that the cheap option is no longer automatically the unhealthy one. Cities, meanwhile, could rebuild the routine activity that has been designed out of children's days, through safe walking routes to school and free access to sports facilities rather than costly clubs.

Neither measure works quickly, and both attract the objection that they interfere with personal choice. But the current situation is not the result of free choice either; it is the result of a food environment that was itself designed. Redesigning it deliberately, and in children's interests, seems the more defensible option.

## 第643篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

In many growing cities, most new homes are now built as flats in high-rise tower blocks rather than as individual houses with gardens. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

As cities absorb more people, a growing proportion of new homes are being built as flats in tower blocks rather than as houses with gardens. I believe the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages, although the balance depends heavily on who the buildings are designed for.

The strongest argument for building upwards concerns land. A city that grows outwards consumes farmland and open countryside, and it also commits its residents to long commutes, because jobs and services cannot follow a population spread thinly across a wide area. Density reverses this. When several hundred households live on one site, a frequent bus route, a school and a row of shops become viable within walking distance, and the cost of supplying water and electricity to each home falls. In that sense a tower block is not only a way of housing people but of making local services affordable.

The drawbacks are real, but they are unevenly distributed. For young professionals and older couples, a well-managed flat is often preferable to a house: it is easier to maintain, more secure and closer to work. Families with small children are in a different position. Without a garden or a safe courtyard, play has to be supervised and planned, and parents on the fifteenth floor cannot simply send a child outside. Tower blocks also depend on shared systems such as lifts, fire doors and communal heating, and when these are neglected the residents have little ability to repair them themselves.

Overall, I think building upwards is the more sensible direction for a crowded city, provided it is not treated as a single solution for everyone. Planners should combine tall blocks for smaller households with lower-rise family housing nearby, so that density is achieved without asking parents to raise children in the sky.

For instance, an accountant who has rested properly after a demanding financial period is likely to make fewer errors and work more efficiently.

Another advantage is that generous annual leave can improve staff loyalty. When employees feel that their employer respects their personal life, they are more likely to feel valued and remain with the company. This benefits businesses because experienced workers understand their roles better and require less training than new recruits. In contrast, organisations that deny adequate holidays may face low morale, frequent absences, and high staff turnover.

Admittedly, some employers may worry that long holidays could disrupt daily operations, especially in small businesses or essential services. However, this problem can be solved through careful scheduling, temporary cover, and fair rotation of leave. Good management should make rest possible without damaging productivity.

In conclusion, I believe that a minimum four-week holiday is not merely a benefit for employees but a practical investment for employers. Well-rested staff are healthier, more focused, and ultimately better at their jobs.

In many large cities, ordinary working people can no longer afford to live near the places where they work. Why has this happened, and what can be done about it?

### 文章

In most prosperous cities, the gap between what a nurse or a bus driver earns and what a flat near their workplace costs has widened to the point where the two no longer meet. This is not a mysterious development; it follows from a straightforward mismatch between how fast cities have grown and how slowly they have built.

The primary cause is that supply has not responded to demand. Successful cities attract workers faster than they add homes, and because land in a city centre is fixed, the only ways to accommodate more people are to build upwards or to build outwards. Both are politically difficult: existing residents object to taller buildings near them, and outward expansion runs into protected land and the cost of extending transport. The result is that a rising number of people compete for a nearly static number of homes, and prices do what prices do.

A second factor is that housing has become an asset as well as a shelter. Once property is widely held as an investment, a large group of existing owners has a direct financial interest in prices continuing to rise, which makes any policy that would lower them electorally unattractive.

The remedies follow from the causes. Cities need to permit substantially more construction close to transport links, which addresses the supply shortage where the demand actually is, and they need public or non-profit housing built at a scale that does not depend on private developers finding it profitable. Both measures would be resisted by current owners, but a city that cannot house the people who run it is failing at something more fundamental than property values.

## 第647篇

Band 7.5

### 题目

In many societies, a growing number of older people live alone and have little regular contact with others. What are the causes of this isolation, and what could be done to reduce it?

### 文章

The number of older people living alone has risen steadily across most wealthy societies, and a significant proportion of them report going several days at a time without speaking to anyone. The causes are partly demographic and partly a matter of how daily life has been reorganised.

The demographic element is straightforward. People live considerably longer than they once did, often outliving a partner by a decade or more, while adult children increasingly move for work rather than remaining in the same town. A parent who would once have aged surrounded by relatives now frequently ages several hours away from the nearest one.

The less obvious cause is the loss of unplanned contact. Much of an ordinary person's social life is not arranged but incidental: colleagues, a familiar shopkeeper, other parents at a school gate. Retirement removes the first of these at a stroke, and the gradual replacement of local shops and services by out-of-town or online alternatives removes many of the rest. What is left has to be deliberately organised, and organising social contact requires energy and confidence that isolation itself steadily erodes.

Useful responses therefore need to rebuild incidental contact rather than schedule it. Shared community facilities within walking distance — a library, a café, a garden — create the low-stakes repeated encounters that friendship actually grows from, in a way that a weekly organised visit does not. Transport matters for the same reason, since an older person who cannot easily leave the house is dependent on others coming to them. Volunteer befriending schemes have value, though they treat the symptom rather than the design fault that produced it.

### 文章

It is argued that although families have a significant influence on children's development, the outside world plays a more important role in their lives. This essay disagrees with this view because parents are children's first teachers and family support has a lasting impact on their personal development.

Families play the most important role in shaping children's personality and values from an early age. The first thing is that parents teach their children basic life skills and moral values such as honesty, kindness, and respect for others. Children usually spend most of their early years at home, so they naturally learn by observing their parents' behaviour. For example, if parents always say "thank you", apologise when they make mistakes, and help their neighbours, their children are likely to copy these behaviours and grow up to become polite and responsible people. Therefore, families provide the foundation for children's future development.

Moreover, parents continue to influence their children by offering guidance and emotional support throughout their lives. When children face difficulties at school or in their personal lives, parents are often the first people to encourage and advise them. This helps children become more confident and resilient when dealing with challenges. For instance, when a student fails an important exam, supportive parents may help them identify their weaknesses, make a study plan, and encourage them to try again instead of giving up. As a result, children learn to overcome setbacks and become more responsible adults.

In conclusion, although schools, friends, and society all influence children's development, I believe that families have the greatest impact because they shape children's character and continue to provide guidance and support throughout their lives.

## 第649篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

In many towns and cities, online retailers have taken a large share of the trade that once went to shops on the high street. Do the advantages of this shift outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Online retailers now take a substantial share of spending that previously went to town-centre shops, and the visible consequence is empty units on high streets. I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages for most shoppers, though not for everyone and not for every town.

The gains to consumers are straightforward. Prices are lower because online sellers avoid the rent and staffing costs of a physical shop, and comparison is instant rather than a matter of walking between three stores. Range is the more significant advantage: a specialist item that no local shop could justify stocking is now routinely available, which matters most to people who do not live in a large city. Delivery also removes a barrier for anyone whose mobility, working hours or caring responsibilities made a shopping trip difficult.

The costs are concentrated rather than shared. Retail employed large numbers of people without formal qualifications, often locally and flexibly, and warehouse and delivery work has not replaced it on equivalent terms. The tax position compounds this, since a business rate levied on floor space falls entirely on the seller who has some. Town centres built around shops become unpleasant when the shops go, and an unpleasant town centre attracts less of everything else. There is a further group that loses outright: people who are not online, or who cannot receive deliveries, find their remaining options shrinking.

Weighing the two sides, the advantages still seem to me larger, because they are enjoyed by almost everyone while the disadvantages fall on smaller groups. But that is an argument for compensating those groups, not for pretending the losses are not real. Town centres that have found other uses for their space are doing considerably better than those still waiting for retail to return.

## 第651篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

In many wealthy countries, a large proportion of the food that is produced is never eaten and ends up being thrown away. What problems does this cause? What measures could be taken to reduce the amount of food that is wasted?

### 文章

A striking amount of the food produced in wealthy countries is grown, processed and transported only to end up in a bin. This causes environmental damage that is easy to underestimate, but it could be reduced considerably if the right changes were made by retailers and governments as well as by households.

The most serious problem is environmental. Growing food requires land, water, fertiliser and fuel, and when that food is thrown away, all of these inputs have been used for nothing. Food that ends up in landfill also decomposes without oxygen and releases methane, a greenhouse gas far more powerful than carbon dioxide over the short term. There is an economic cost as well: households pay for food they never eat, and councils pay to collect and bury it.

Several measures could reduce this waste. Supermarkets could be discouraged from multi-buy promotions that tempt people to buy more than they can use, and required to sell more loose produce so that customers can buy exactly the quantity they want. The date labels on packaging could be simplified, since many people throw away food which is past its 'best before' date but still perfectly safe to eat it. Governments could also require large retailers to donate unsold edible food to charities, as some countries already do. Finally, separate collection of food waste would allow whatever cannot be avoided to be turned into compost or energy instead of methane.

Food waste is often treated as a matter of individual carelessness, but much of it is built into the way food is sold. Households still have a part to play, but they are largely responding to incentives that others have set. For this reason, changing the rules for retailers is likely to achieve more than simply asking consumers to be more careful.

In many modern societies, young adults are choosing to have children later than previous generations. Although delaying childbirth can bring some clear advantages, I believe its disadvantages may be greater if people postpone it for too long. This essay will discuss both sides before presenting my opinion.

To begin with, having babies later can allow adults to become more financially and emotionally prepared. For example, people who spend their twenties building a career may have a stable income, secure housing, and greater confidence before raising a child. As a result, they may provide better education, healthcare, and living conditions for their children. Therefore, delayed parenthood can create a more secure family environment when it is carefully planned.

However, there are also significant drawbacks to having children much later in life. For instance, older parents may face higher medical risks during pregnancy and may also have less physical energy to care for young children. Moreover, if adults delay parenthood mainly because of work pressure, they may find it difficult to balance family responsibilities with demanding careers. Consequently, late parenthood can create stress for both parents and children, especially when support systems are weak.

In conclusion, having babies later can be beneficial because it gives adults time to gain maturity and financial security. Nevertheless, I believe the negative effects can outweigh the positives when people delay parenthood excessively. ### 题目

In some areas, libraries, parks and community centres that were once run by paid council staff are now managed by local volunteers. Some people believe this is the best way to keep such services open, while others argue that local government should pay professionals to run them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

As local authority budgets have tightened, many councils have handed libraries, parks and community centres to groups of residents who run them without pay. Supporters see this as the only realistic way to keep such places open, while critics argue that running them is a basic duty of local government. I believe volunteers can enrich these services but should not be expected to replace the people paid to provide them.

The case for volunteer management is stronger than it first appears. When the alternative is closure, a library open three days a week with volunteer staff is clearly preferable to a locked building. Residents who give their time also tend to develop a sense of ownership that a council department rarely inspires; they notice when a play area is damaged, and they organise events that reflect what their neighbours actually want. For retired people in particular, volunteering can provide a routine and a social role they might otherwise lack.

Nevertheless, there are good reasons to treat these services as a public responsibility. A librarian does far more than lend books: she helps people complete job applications, teaches basic computer skills and recognises when a regular visitor needs support from other agencies. Such work requires training and continuity, and a rota of volunteers, however committed, cannot guarantee either. Volunteers are also easier to find in comfortable neighbourhoods than in deprived ones. There is, too, a question of fairness, since residents are effectively being asked to donate labour for a service their taxes were supposed to fund.

In my view, the best arrangement is a small core of professional staff, supported by volunteers who extend opening hours and run additional activities. This retains the expertise and reliability that the public is entitled to while still drawing on the energy of the local people. Handing a service entirely to volunteers should be treated as an emergency measure, not as a model.

## 第655篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

In some countries, cash is being replaced almost entirely by digital payment. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Several countries are now close to abandoning cash altogether, and some shops and buses no longer accept it. On balance I consider this a positive development, with the important qualification that the people it disadvantages are almost invisible in the figures used to justify it.

The benefits are easy to see and are widely shared. Digital payment is faster, cheaper to handle than notes and coins, and far harder to steal in quantity; a lost card can be cancelled while lost cash cannot. Businesses save the time and expense of counting, banking and insuring their takings. Because transactions leave a record, undeclared income and cash-in-hand employment become harder to sustain, and that same record gives ordinary households something they never previously had, which is a reliable account of their own spending.

The costs fall on particular groups rather than on everybody a little. Older people who never adopted smartphones, those without bank accounts, and anyone whose income is too irregular for a bank to want them are excluded from ordinary transactions rather than merely inconvenienced. A cashless system is also a single point of failure: a network outage stops commerce completely in a way that a few card terminals failing never used to. And every purchase becomes data belonging to somebody else. That data is valuable, and nobody has explained why the person who generated it should not own it.

I still think the direction of travel is right, because the gains are large and the exclusions are fixable. But they are only fixable deliberately, through a legal duty to accept cash or through basic accounts that are genuinely universal, and the countries that have simply allowed cash to disappear have not fixed them.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence has raised questions about whether highly advanced robots should be regarded as people rather than machines. While some argue that robots capable of thinking, learning and expressing emotions deserve human-like recognition, I believe they should remain distinct from humans because their behaviour is ultimately created through technology.

On the one hand, robots that possess human-like intelligence and emotions could arguably be considered persons. If a robot can learn from experience and think independently, it may be capable of making its own decisions rather than simply following basic instructions. Moreover, the ability to understand and express emotions could enable such machines to communicate naturally and form meaningful relationships with humans. As a result, treating an intelligent and emotionally aware robot merely as an object may seem unfair, particularly if its behaviour is indistinguishable from that of a human.

On the other hand, I believe that even highly sophisticated robots should still be regarded as machines because their abilities originate from human-designed technology. Their thoughts, responses and emotional expressions are generated through programming and algorithms, meaning that apparent emotions may simply be simulations rather than genuine feelings. For example, a robot may express sadness when a person dies, but this does not necessarily prove that it experiences grief in the same way as a human. Therefore, human-like behaviour alone is insufficient to give robots the same moral and legal status as people.

In conclusion, although advanced robots may behave remarkably like humans, I believe they should remain classified as machines unless it can be established that they genuinely possess consciousness and emotions.

When both parents are in full-time work, the care of a pre-school child has to be arranged by someone. Many families turn to grandparents, while others prefer a registered nursery. I think the two settings supply genuinely different things, and that which one is better depends on what a particular child is short of.

The case for grandparents is partly emotional and partly practical. A grandparent already has a relationship with the child, offers a ratio of attention no institution can match, and provides continuity of place and routine that very young children visibly rely on. There is also the question of cost: full-time nursery fees consume a substantial share of an average salary, and for many households family care is not a preference but the only arrangement that leaves working worthwhile. A grandmother who collects a child three afternoons a week is frequently the reason a second income exists at all.

Nurseries, by contrast, offer things a home cannot. Staff are trained to notice developmental delays early, at an age when intervention is most effective. More importantly, a nursery provides other children. Learning to negotiate, to wait and to lose an argument with an equal is difficult to practise with an adult who is willing to give way, and children who arrive at school without that practice are often the ones who struggle first.

My own view is that the second consideration is decisive for most children. Affection can be supplied at either setting and outside working hours in any case, whereas regular contact with a peer group cannot easily be improvised. I would therefore favour nursery care for the year or two before school, without pretending that every family has the means to choose it.

## 第659篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Increasingly, people pay a monthly subscription to use products such as software, cars, furniture and even clothing, instead of buying them outright. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Paying monthly for access to a product, rather than buying it once, has spread from software to cars, furniture and even children's clothing. On the whole I regard this as a negative development, although there are cases where a subscription is genuinely the better arrangement.

The strongest argument in its favour is that some products are not really finished when they are sold. Software needs regular security updates, and a car needs servicing and eventually replacing; a subscription that bundles these costs into a predictable monthly payment spares the customer an unexpected bill. Subscriptions also lower the barrier to entry, since a household can use an expensive appliance without having the savings to buy it, and they suit people who need something only for a limited period, such as parents of a baby who will outgrow its cot within a year.

The problems begin when the model is applied to products that need no ongoing support. A sofa or a dining table does not change after delivery, yet a subscription turns it into a payment that never ends, and over its lifetime the customer usually pays far more than the purchase price. More seriously, the balance of power shifts to the company. It can raise the price, remove features or change the terms, and the customer's only option is to cancel and lose access to something they may have paid for several times over. Many services also rely on people forgetting what they have signed up to, and makes cancellation deliberately awkward.

For these reasons I believe the trend is more harmful than helpful. Subscriptions make sense for products that require continuous service, but for most physical goods they are simply a more expensive and less secure way of owning nothing. Consumers would benefit from rules requiring that cancelling be as easy as signing up.

In many countries, a small countries od people earn extremely high salaries. Some people believe that this is good for the country, but others think that governmnets should not allow salaries above a certain level. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any revelant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

### 文章

In many countries, a relatively small proportion of people earn exceptionally high salaries. While some argue that such substantial incomes benefit society and the national economy, others believe that governments should impose a maximum limit on individual earnings. This essay will examine both perspectives before arguing that, although excessive inequality can be problematic, governments should generally avoid setting an upper salary limit.

On the one hand, allowing people to earn very high incomes can provide significant economic benefits. In competitive industries, substantial salaries can attract talented professionals and encourage individuals to acquire valuable skills, work harder and take greater risks. For example, highly qualified doctors, engineers and technology specialists may be more likely to remain in a country if they can receive internationally competitive remuneration. Moreover, successful entrepreneurs and business leaders often generate employment and investment, meaning that their personal wealth can contribute indirectly to broader economic growth. High salaries can therefore act as an incentive for innovation, productivity and entrepreneurship.

On the other hand, extremely large differences in income can create serious social problems. When a small minority accumulates enormous wealth while ordinary workers struggle to meet basic living costs, people may perceive the economic system as fundamentally unfair. This can contribute to social tension and reduce public trust in institutions. Furthermore, excessive concentrations of wealth may give affluent individuals disproportionate political and economic influence. For these reasons, some people believe that governments should prevent salaries from exceeding a predetermined level and redistribute surplus income to fund public services such as healthcare and education.

In my view, however, imposing a legal ceiling on salaries would be unnecessarily restrictive and could have unintended consequences. Rather than limiting how much people can earn, governments should use progressive taxation to ensure that those with the greatest financial capacity make a proportionately larger contribution to society. This approach preserves the incentive to work, innovate and invest while simultaneously reducing extreme inequality.

In conclusion, very high salaries can encourage talent, innovation and economic development, whereas excessive income inequality can undermine social cohesion. I therefore believe that progressive taxation and effective public spending are preferable to imposing an absolute limit on individual earnings.

## 第661篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

It is now common for people to change careers several times during their working lives. Why is this happening? Do you think it is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

A working life spent in a single occupation, once the norm, is now unusual in most developed economies. The shift has both an external cause and an internal one, and although it imposes real costs on individuals, I regard it overall as a positive development.

The external cause is that occupations themselves are less stable than they were. Automation and offshoring have removed whole categories of clerical, manufacturing and administrative work within a single generation, and the industries replacing them require different skills rather than the same skills applied elsewhere. Somebody whose trade disappears at forty does not choose to retrain; the alternative is unemployment.

The internal cause is a change in what people expect from work. Where a previous generation valued security above almost everything, many workers now treat a job as something that ought to develop them, and they are far more willing to leave when it stops doing so. The growth of flexible online study has made acting on that impulse realistic, since a qualification can be acquired alongside existing employment rather than instead of it.

The costs are obvious enough. Changing field usually means a drop in earnings and in seniority, and the permanent possibility of change is a source of anxiety, particularly for those with dependants or mortgages. But the alternative was never security for everyone; it was security for those whose industry happened to survive. A workforce that expects to retrain absorbs technological change far better than one built around jobs for life, and individuals who can move are less trapped by a single employer than those who cannot.

On balance, then, the development is positive, provided that governments treat retraining as a normal stage of a career rather than as emergency relief for the unlucky.

## 第663篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Large quantities of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans every year. What do you think are the main reasons for this, and what could be done to address the situation?

### 文章

Every year an enormous volume of plastic finds its way from land into the sea, where it breaks into fragments that are effectively impossible to retrieve. The reasons are partly to do with how much plastic we produce and partly to do with what happens to it afterwards.

The first reason is that single-use plastic is extraordinarily cheap to make and almost worthless to collect. A drinks bottle costs a manufacturer very little, so there is no commercial incentive to design it for reuse, and once discarded it is worth so little that recovering it rarely pays for itself. The second reason is that waste infrastructure has not kept pace with consumption. Many fast-growing cities acquired supermarket packaging long before they acquired the collection networks to deal with it, and uncollected waste near a river will eventually reach the ocean whatever anyone intends.

The most effective responses therefore work at the point of production. Requiring manufacturers to fund the collection and disposal of their own packaging changes the arithmetic: a company that must pay to retrieve its bottles has a reason to use fewer of them, or to design them so that retrieving them is cheaper. This should be combined with sustained investment in collection systems in the places where the leakage into rivers is greatest, since better product design cannot help a city that has nowhere to put its rubbish.

Consumer behaviour matters too, though probably less than campaigns suggest. Individual refusal of plastic bags is worth encouraging, but it operates on a fraction of the total volume, and treating the issue as a matter of personal virtue risks distracting from the regulatory changes that would make a measurable difference.

Forests are being cleared for agriculture, urban expansion, mining, and infrastructure projects, leaving many species without food, shelter, or breeding grounds. For example, large areas of tropical rainforests have been cut down for commercial farming, threatening the survival of numerous birds, insects, and mammals. Pollution is another major factor. Industrial waste, plastic pollution, and chemical pesticides contaminate rivers, oceans, and soil, harming both aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems.

Climate change has also accelerated the loss of biodiversity. Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall patterns, droughts, floods, and wildfires make it difficult for many species to survive in their traditional habitats. In addition, illegal hunting, overfishing, and the wildlife trade have dramatically reduced populations of many endangered animals. These activities disturb the natural balance of ecosystems and weaken biodiversity.

Several measures can help solve this problem. Governments should enforce strict laws against deforestation, poaching, and pollution, and companies that damage the environment should face heavy penalties. Protecting forests, wetlands, national parks, and marine reserves is essential for preserving natural habitats. Sustainable farming and fishing practices should also be encouraged to reduce pressure on ecosystems. Furthermore, public education plays a crucial role. People are more likely to support conservation efforts when they understand the importance of biodiversity and the long-term consequences of environmental destruction. For instance, awareness campaigns about plastic waste have encouraged many communities to reduce single-use plastics and participate in recycling programmes.

In conclusion, the decline in animals and plants is mainly caused by habitat loss, pollution, climate change, and overexploitation of natural resources. However, this issue can be mitigated through stronger environmental laws, habitat conservation, sustainable practices, and greater public awareness. Immediate action is necessary to protect biodiversity and preserve the natural environment for future generations.

## 第665篇

### 题目

Many companies now allow their staff to work from home for most of the week. Some people think this arrangement benefits employees, while others argue that it harms teamwork and the training of younger staff. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Home working, which was an emergency measure only a few years ago, has become a permanent arrangement at many firms. Some regard it as a clear improvement in employees' lives, while others believe it undermines collaboration and leaves junior staff without proper training. My own view is that both effects are real, but that they fall on different people.

The benefits to the individual worker are easy to establish. A commute of an hour each way consumes ten hours of an ordinary week, and returning that time to the employee improves sleep, health and family life at no cost to the employer. Home working also removes the low-level interruptions that make concentrated work difficult in an open-plan office, which is why many people report finishing demanding tasks faster at home than in the building they were hired to sit in.

The objection is that the value of an office was never really the desk. Colleagues overhear each other's problems, correct each other's assumptions and pass on judgement that nobody would think to write down. A new graduate learns the unwritten parts of a job by being present while it is done, and scheduled video calls capture almost none of this. Teams also lose the informal contact that resolves small misunderstandings before they become formal disputes.

In my view the arrangement suits experienced staff and disadvantages inexperienced ones. Someone who already knows the work and the people loses very little by leaving the building; someone still learning both loses a great deal. The sensible response is therefore not to choose between the two positions but to apply them differently, requiring far more office attendance in the first years of a career than in the twentieth.

Finally, psychological support should be provided to athletes to help them manage stress and performance pressure without relying on harmful substances.

In conclusion, the rise in the use of banned substances in professional sports is mainly caused by competitive pressure, financial incentives, and insufficient awareness. ## 第667篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Many countries invest heavily in training doctors, engineers and other skilled professionals, only for large numbers of them to emigrate soon after qualifying. Why does this happen, and what measures could reduce it?

### 文章

It is a painful arithmetic for a poorer country: the state pays to train a surgeon over a decade, and a wealthier health service acquires the finished professional at no cost at all. Understanding why this happens matters more than deploring it, because the reasons point directly at what might be changed.

The obvious driver is income. A specialist can often earn several times more abroad, and the difference is large enough that no realistic domestic pay rise would close it. But money alone explains less than it appears to. Surveys of emigrating professionals consistently place working conditions, career progression and the ability to practise properly alongside salary, and often above it. A doctor who cannot obtain basic supplies is not only underpaid; they are prevented from doing the job they trained for, which is a different and in some ways more corrosive frustration.

This suggests that the more promising measures are not financial at all. Investment in the equipment, staffing and management that allow professionals to work effectively addresses the frustration directly, and it does so at a cost far below matching foreign salaries. Clear promotion structures matter for the same reason: much emigration occurs when a capable person can see no path upward at home.

Bonded service agreements, in which graduates repay subsidised training through a period of domestic work, have a place, but a limited one. They can recover the public investment, and they may retain someone long enough for circumstances to improve. What they cannot do is make a frustrating job satisfying, and a professional who is compelled to stay is not necessarily a professional who works well.

## 第669篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Many countries spend large amounts of public money on hosting international sporting events. Some people believe that this money is wasted. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Hosting a World Cup or an Olympic Games now costs the host nation billions, and the bill is paid by taxpayers most of whom will never attend an event. I agree that much of this spending is wasted, though I would argue that the waste lies in what gets built rather than in the decision to host.

The strongest case against hosting is the record of what is left behind. Stadiums designed for a fortnight of capacity crowds are handed to cities with no permanent use for them, and their upkeep falls on local budgets for decades afterwards. The promised tourism boom is harder to detect than the bid documents suggest, partly because ordinary visitors avoid a city during the event itself. Money committed to these projects is also money not committed to housing or hospitals, and that trade-off is rarely put to voters in those terms before a bid is submitted.

There are real returns, but they are narrower than supporters claim. Transport links and drainage built for an event outlast it and serve residents afterwards, and a well-run tournament can change how a country is perceived, which has value that is genuine even if it resists measurement. The difficulty is that these gains come from the infrastructure and the organisation rather than from the ceremony, and they can usually be obtained without the ceremony.

My conclusion is that the waste is avoidable rather than inherent. A country that builds only what it would have wanted anyway, and hires venues instead of erecting them, can host well. A country that treats the event as a reason to build monuments is wasting public money, and most hosts, faced with that choice, have chosen the second path.

## 第671篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Many developing countries have built their economies around large-scale international tourism. Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Several countries have made international tourism the centre of their development strategy rather than one component of it. In my view the advantages of doing so do outweigh the disadvantages, but only where the country retains some control over how the industry grows.

The economic argument is difficult to dismiss. Tourism produces foreign currency quickly, requires less initial capital than manufacturing, and creates work at every skill level, from construction to hotel management. Nor is the workforce a barrier: hotel and hospitality skills can be taught in months, whereas building a manufacturing base takes a generation. For a country with beaches or ruins and little else to export, it is often the only sector in which it starts with an advantage. The revenue is also visible: airport taxes, licensing and hotel levies are far easier to collect than income tax in a largely informal economy.

The disadvantages, though, are structural rather than incidental. Much of the money leaves again almost immediately, because international chains and foreign tour operators repatriate their profits, and an all-inclusive resort is designed so that guests spend nothing outside of it. Meanwhile the jobs available to local people cluster at the bottom, seasonal and poorly paid. Land prices near attractive coastlines rise beyond what residents can pay, and a monoculture economy is dangerously exposed: a single security incident or a change in fashion can empty a country's hotels for a year.

Even so, I would keep the judgement in tourism's favour, because the alternatives available to most of these economies are worse. Where governments have insisted on local ownership, capped development and taxed the sector properly, tourism has funded genuine improvements in infrastructure. The disadvantages are largely the result of how the industry is regulated, and regulation can be changed.

## 第673篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Many major museums hold objects that were removed from other countries in the past. Some people believe these objects should be returned to their countries of origin, while others argue they are better preserved and more widely seen where they are. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

A significant proportion of the objects in the world's largest museums left their countries of origin under colonial administration. Some argue they should now be returned; others contend that they are better conserved and more widely seen in the institutions that currently hold them. I find the case for return stronger, although not for the reason usually given.

The argument for restitution rests on how the objects were obtained. Many were taken during military occupation or under administrations that the local population had no part in choosing, and consent given under those conditions is not consent in any meaningful sense. There is also a question of access that is rarely acknowledged: a citizen of the country an object came from often has to obtain a visa and buy an international flight to see it, while a resident of the holding city can walk in free of charge.

The case for retention deserves a fair hearing. Large museums do possess conservation laboratories, climate control and specialist expertise that not every claimant country can match, and they place objects in comparative displays that make connections a single national collection cannot. Millions of visitors a year is not a trivial argument when the alternative might be a far smaller audience. There is also the practical matter of transport, since moving fragile objects across continents carries a genuine risk of damage.

The difficulty is that this defence has weakened considerably. Several claimant countries have built modern museums to international standards specifically to receive returned objects, so the preservation argument no longer applies to them, whatever its force fifty years ago. My view is that where a country can demonstrate adequate facilities, the manner of acquisition should settle the matter, and the objects should go home.

## 第675篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Many patients do not follow the advice they are given by their doctors. Why does this happen? What are the consequences of this behaviour?

### 文章

Studies of prescribed treatment consistently find that a large proportion of patients stop taking medication early or never begin it at all. The behaviour looks irrational from the outside, but it usually has understandable causes, and its consequences reach well beyond the individual concerned.

The commonest cause is that the reasoning behind the advice is never transmitted. A consultation lasting a few minutes leaves time to issue an instruction but not to explain why a course of antibiotics must be finished, or why blood-pressure tablets are needed by somebody who feels perfectly well. Advice that arrives without a reason is easy to abandon as soon as the symptoms disappear.

Two further causes matter. Side effects are experienced immediately while the benefit of treatment is invisible and delayed, so a patient weighing certain nausea against a hypothetical stroke in twenty years often decides against the medicine. And where the advice requires a change of habits rather than a tablet — losing weight, giving up alcohol, exercising daily — compliance demands sustained effort in an environment that offers very little support for it.

The consequences are serious at both levels. For the patient, a partially treated condition frequently returns in a worse form, and admission to hospital costs far more, in suffering as well as money, than the treatment that was declined. For the health system, non-adherence wastes the medicines dispensed, fills beds that need not have been filled, and drives the spread of drug-resistant infection when antibiotic courses are abandoned halfway. There is also a slower effect on the consultation itself, since doctors who expect their advice to be ignored tend to invest less in explaining it.

Non-adherence is therefore best understood not as stubbornness but as a predictable response to advice that has been issued rather than explained.

Social media shows ordinary travellers what a place actually looks like, rather than only what a tourist board chooses to publish, and it has drawn attention to towns and landscapes that traditional guidebooks ignored. The visitors lose something too, since a trip planned around recreating a particular photograph leaves little room for anything unplanned.

It is true that careful travellers can use these platforms for finding quieter alternatives. In conclusion, I firmly believe that teenagers who commit major crimes should face the same legal consequences as adults, since this approach both deters future offending and delivers fair justice to victims.

## 第679篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Many people with physical disabilities find it difficult to travel for pleasure, even within their own country. What problems do they face, and what measures could be taken to make travel easier for them?

### 文章

For many people with physical disabilities, a trip that others would organise in an evening requires weeks of preparation and still carries a real risk of failure. The obstacles are partly physical, but in my view the more serious problem is that disabled travellers cannot rely on the information they are given, and this is where measures should be aimed first.

The physical barriers are the most visible. Older railway stations frequently have platforms reachable only by stairs, many coaches have no space for a wheelchair, and historic town centres are paved with cobbles that make independent movement exhausting. However, a barrier that is known about can at least be planned around. What makes travel genuinely daunting is uncertainty: a hotel advertised as 'accessible' may turn out to have a shower that cannot be used from a wheelchair, and a lift shown on a station map may have been out of service for weeks. A single failure of this kind can leave a traveller stranded far from home, so many people conclude that the trip is not worth the risk.

The solutions should therefore match these two problems. For physical access, the most practical step is to require that every renovation of a station, museum or hotel includes step-free access, since rebuilding everything at once is unaffordable but renovation happens constantly. For information, accessibility claims should be independently checked and described in concrete terms — the width of a door, the height of a bed, whether a shower has a step — rather than summarised by a single reassuring symbol. Operators could also be obliged to publish live updates about lifts which is not working. Finally, companion tickets should be free, as the need for an assistant effectively doubles the cost of every journey.

None of these measures is especially expensive, and together they would turn travel from a gamble into something that can be planned. That, rather than perfect access everywhere, is a realistic aim for the next decade.

One major advantage is that individuals can have more time travelling during working days, which can positively affect their job satisfaction. In addition, the improvement of employees’ productivity is another important advantage. If this trend continues, it is likely to lead to better performance of the whole company. For instance, people who can work remotely while travelling with their families may feel higher levels of job satisfaction, as a result, their responsibility to their tasks would improve significantly.

In conclusion, although this issue can bring both pros and cons, I believe its benefits outweigh the negative points because they have more long-lasting and widespread impacts, particularly in terms of workforce productivity and job satisfaction.

## 第681篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Most people are now aware of the environmental damage caused by air travel, yet the number of flights taken each year continues to rise. Why do people keep flying? What should be done about this?

### 文章

Air travel is one of the few forms of consumption whose environmental cost is widely understood and yet almost universally ignored. Passenger numbers have grown for decades despite constant publicity about emissions, and the explanation lies in economics and in psychology rather than in ignorance.

The economic half is straightforward. Aviation fuel is untaxed in most jurisdictions and international tickets usually escape sales tax, so a seat on a plane is priced well below the cost it imposes on everyone else. When a flight across a continent costs less than a rail ticket over the same route, consumers are not choosing to pollute; they are choosing the cheaper of two options, and the price signal is telling them the wrong thing.

The psychological half concerns scale. An individual passenger knows that their absence would not ground the aircraft, so the connection between the decision and the damage feels theoretical. Flying is also concentrated in exactly those parts of life people are least willing to sacrifice — seeing relatives abroad, a holiday earned over a year, work that cannot be done remotely — and abstract responsibility rarely wins against a specific and immediate reason to travel.

Effective policy therefore has to change the price rather than the attitude. Taxing aviation fuel on the same basis as petrol, and adding a levy that rises steeply with the number of flights a person takes in a year, would target frequent travellers without penalising the family that flies once. The revenue could then be used to make rail competitive on short routes, where the alternative already exists and only the cost prevents people from using it.

Individuals will not solve this by feeling guilty. They will change when the cheapest option stops being the most damaging one.

## 第683篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Most people now receive their news through social media rather than through newspapers or broadcasters. Some believe this has made public debate more open, while others think it has left people less well informed. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

It is now more common to encounter a news story on a social platform than in a newspaper or a scheduled bulletin. Supporters argue that this has widened access to public debate, while critics maintain that it has left audiences worse informed. I believe the second position is closer to the truth, although the first identifies a genuine gain.

The argument for openness rests on who controls what counts as news. Under the older model, a small number of editors decided which stories reached the public, and communities without a sympathetic newsroom were effectively invisible. Social platforms removed that gatekeeping almost overnight. Eyewitness footage of protests and natural disasters now reaches an international audience within minutes, often before professional reporters arrive, and campaigns that would once have been ignored can build support without any institutional backing. A story can now begin with a single witness and end in a parliamentary debate without ever passing an editor's desk.

The counter-argument is that access to more material is not the same as understanding more. Platforms rank posts by engagement rather than accuracy, so a confident falsehood usually travels further than a careful correction. Users are also shown material that resembles what they have already approved of, which narrows exposure over time. The result is an audience that feels well informed while encountering a steadily smaller share of the available evidence.

On balance, I find the critical view more persuasive. The gain in access is real, but it is a gain in supply, whereas the loss is a loss of judgement, and judgement is the harder thing to rebuild. Social media has made it far easier to see what is happening and considerably harder to work out what it means.

## 第685篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

News organisations sometimes publish stories that later turn out to be false. Some people believe that the law should require corrections to be given the same prominence as the original story. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

News organisations make mistakes, and a false story can do lasting damage long before anyone establishes that it was false. I broadly agree that corrections should be legally required to match the prominence of the original report, although I would limit the requirement to stories that caused identifiable harm.

The argument in favour is essentially about reach. A story printed on a front page or pushed to millions of phones is seen by an audience that a paragraph on an inside page will never reach, so a correction published quietly does not undo the error; it merely allows the publisher to claim that it has been undone. Where a false report has damaged a person's reputation or a company's trade, leaving the scale of the remedy to the publisher's discretion is unlikely to produce a fair result, because the publisher has an obvious interest in keeping the admission small.

The objection is that a rigid rule would be costly to apply. Newsrooms produce a great deal of material and much of it contains small inaccuracies, a misspelled name or a wrong figure, that nobody would seriously want on the front page. A law drafted without a threshold would either be ignored or would push editors towards caution, which is not the same as accuracy. This is an argument for defining harm carefully, though, rather than for leaving the matter to the industry.

My view is therefore that the requirement should exist but should be triggered by consequence rather than by error. Where a false story has measurably harmed someone, the correction should be as loud as the accusation. Where it has not, ordinary editorial judgement is enough, and the law has no business intervening.

### 文章

It is often argued that all towns and cities should have large public outdoor spaces, such as parks and squares. I strongly agree with this view because these areas provide valuable opportunities for physical activity and relaxation while also encouraging social interaction and stronger community connections.

On the one hand, public outdoor spaces are highly beneficial for people's physical and mental well-being. Parks and open areas give residents a convenient place to walk, exercise and relax, which is especially important in densely populated cities where private outdoor space may be limited. For example, an office worker can visit a nearby park after work to walk or exercise, while children can play safely outdoors. By providing opportunities for regular physical activity and relaxation, such spaces can improve fitness and reduce everyday stress. Therefore, public parks and squares can make urban life healthier and more pleasant.

Another important benefit is that public spaces encourage social interaction. Unlike private facilities, parks and squares are generally accessible to people from different social and economic backgrounds. Community events, weekend markets and cultural festivals can bring local residents together in the same place. For instance, a neighbourhood market held in a public square can give residents an opportunity to meet their neighbours and develop social connections. This can reduce isolation and create a stronger sense of community. Although finding large areas of land may be difficult in crowded cities, the social and health benefits make public outdoor spaces a worthwhile investment.

In conclusion, I strongly agree that towns and cities should provide large public outdoor spaces. They support physical and mental well-being while also creating opportunities for social interaction, making urban communities healthier and more connected.

## 第687篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

People in many countries now depend heavily on their smartphones. Why has this happened? What effects does this dependence have on individuals and on society?

### 文章

Few technologies have been adopted as completely as the smartphone, and few have become as difficult to do without. The reasons are partly technical and partly social, and the consequences are visible both in individual behaviour and in the way institutions now operate.

Technically, the phone succeeded because it absorbed everything else. A single device replaced the camera, the map, the music player, the alarm clock and the wallet, and it did so at a price that fell steadily while mobile networks became fast enough to make it useful anywhere. Once one object performs a dozen functions, leaving it at home is not a small inconvenience but a dozen of them at once.

Socially, the dependence deepened because services began to assume it. Banks moved authentication onto phones, employers moved rotas and messages onto them, and schools began sending information to parents the same way. A person without a smartphone is now excluded from arrangements they never agreed to, which is a very different situation from simply missing a useful gadget.

The effects follow from that dual role. For individuals, the gain in convenience is real, but attention has fragmented: work reaches people in the evening, and the habit of filling every idle moment has made sustained concentration noticeably harder. For society, the more serious effect is the exclusion of those who cannot use or afford the technology — older people in particular — from services that once had a counter or a telephone line. There is also a concentration of power in the few companies whose operating systems mediate almost all of this activity.

The smartphone is therefore not simply a popular product. It has become infrastructure, and the problems it creates are the problems of infrastructure that nobody planned as such.

Learning a few basic customs, such as how to greet people and how to behave during religious occasions, takes very little time and prevents serious misunderstandings. Therefore, even a short stay is a good reason to learn the essentials.

In conclusion, I largely agree that foreigners should know something about the culture of the country they live in. Although learning about its history in depth may not be necessary for everyone, understanding basic traditions helps them avoid offending others and build better relationships.

## 第689篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Some cities have made all public transport free to use, paying for it through taxation instead of fares. Do you think this is a positive or negative development?

### 文章

A small number of cities have abolished fares on their buses, trams and trains, funding the whole system from taxation instead. I regard this as a positive development overall, although its success depends heavily on how the lost fare income is replaced.

The strongest argument for free travel is a social one. Fares take a far larger share of a low income than of a high one, so for cleaners, carers and students the cost of reaching work or college can decide whether a job or a course is worth to take at all. Removing fares turns public transport into a genuinely universal service, in the same way as a public library or a pavement. There are practical gains too: boarding is quicker when nobody has to buy a ticket, and the considerable expense of selling and checking tickets simply disappears.

There is also an environmental case. If travelling by bus costs nothing, some drivers will be persuaded to leave their cars at home, which reduces both emissions and the demand for parking in the city centre. Critics respond that a free service will soon become overcrowded, and that taxpayers who never use it are being asked to subsidise those who do. The first objection is serious, since a crowded and unreliable bus is not attractive at any price. The second is weaker, because people who never drive already pay through their taxes for roads they do not use.

For these reasons I believe free public transport is a positive step, but only when the city increases its spending on the network rather than simply redistributing it. If abolishing fares leads to fewer buses running less often, the people it was meant to help will be left with a service that is free and yet far less useful.

## 第691篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Some countries are considering reducing the standard working week from five days to four, with no reduction in pay. Do the advantages of this change outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Reducing the standard week to four days without cutting pay is no longer a fringe proposal, and a number of employers have now tried it. In my view the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but the case rests on an empirical claim that does not hold everywhere.

The argument in favour is not really about happiness. It is that a substantial part of a five-day week is not productive: hours spent in meetings that exist because there is time for them, and attention that has degraded by the fourth consecutive day. Trials in office-based organisations have generally reported that output held steady, which suggests the fifth day was buying less than the payroll implied. The benefits to employees are then genuine additions rather than a transfer — more recovery time, fewer commuting days, and a workforce that is measurably less exhausted.

The difficulty is that this reasoning is specific to a kind of work. Where output is a direct function of hours present — a ward, a production line, a delivery round — removing a day removes the corresponding output, and the only way to maintain the service is to hire more people at the same wage. For those employers the change is simply a large increase in labour costs. There is a further complication: compressing five days of work into four is not the same policy at all, and where employers do this the health benefits largely disappear. Small firms with no slack are also poorly placed to absorb any of it.

On balance I still support the change, because the sectors where it works are large and the sectors where it does not can be treated differently. A blanket four-day week would be unwise. A four-day week as the default, with exceptions where the arithmetic genuinely does not work, would capture most of the benefit.

## 第693篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Some governments are moving ministries and other public bodies out of the capital city to smaller towns and regions. Do the advantages of this policy outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Several governments have begun relocating ministries and agencies from their capitals to provincial towns, arguing that public employment should be shared more evenly across the country. Although the policy carries real costs, I believe its advantages outweigh them, provided that it is carried out gradually.

The strongest argument in favour is economic. In many countries the capital absorbs a disproportionate share of well-paid, secure jobs, and talented young people from the regions have little choice but to follow them. A relocated department reverses this flow: it brings hundreds of stable salaries to a town, and those salaries support local shops, schools and services, transforming the local economy within a few years. The move also relieves pressure on the capital, where office rents and housing costs are usually highest, and it may produce a civil service that understands life beyond the capital rather better than it currently does.

The disadvantages are nonetheless significant. Moving an organisation is expensive, and the savings on rent can take many years to repay the initial cost. More seriously, many experienced staff refuse to relocate, particularly those with partners in jobs they cannot leave or children settled in schools, and the knowledge they take with them can leave a department weakened for years. There is also a risk that the move becomes symbolic, with routine work sent to the regions while the senior officials who make decisions stay close to ministers in the capital.

On balance, the benefits are more lasting than the costs. Relocation costs are paid once, and a department that loses experienced staff can rebuild its expertise, whereas the concentration of opportunity in a single city damages the rest of the country permanently. If the move is phased so that staff can transfer voluntarily or retire in the normal way, most of the disruption can be avoided.

## 第695篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Some governments now fund university places only in subjects that lead directly to employment. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Public money for higher education is finite, and several governments have responded by directing it towards degrees with clear employment outcomes. I largely agree with this approach, although I would argue that judging a subject purely by the salaries of its graduates is too narrow a test of its worth.

The case for prioritising vocational and technical degrees is essentially practical. A country that trains too few nurses, engineers or software developers has to import that expertise at a premium, while graduates in oversupplied fields compete for the work they are overqualified for. Public funding is also a transfer from taxpayers, most of whom never attended university, and it is reasonable for them to expect a visible return in the form of services they actually use. Concentrating subsidy where shortages can be measured is therefore a defensible use of limited resources.

The difficulty is that employability is a poor predictor of long-term usefulness. Skills that look indispensable today can be automated within a decade, whereas the analytical and interpretive habits developed in history, philosophy or languages transfer across many roles. There is also a public interest that no salary figure captures: a society with no historians loses the ability to examine itself. These disciplines are also cheap to teach, so withdrawing support from them saves relatively little while risking a great deal.

My own view is that funding should follow demonstrated national shortages, but with a protected minimum for subjects that would otherwise disappear from the system altogether. Employment should guide public spending on universities without being allowed to dictate it entirely.

Some people argue that offenders who have committed non-violent crimes should serve their sentences in the community rather than in prison. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Prison populations have grown steadily in many countries while reoffending rates have not fallen, which has revived the argument for dealing with non-violent offenders outside custody. I broadly agree with this, though the case rests on effectiveness rather than on leniency, and it does not extend to every non-violent crime.

The first reason concerns reoffending. A short custodial sentence is long enough to cost someone a job, a tenancy and often a set of family relationships, but far too short for any meaningful rehabilitation. The person released is therefore less employable and more isolated than the person imprisoned, which is close to an ideal set of conditions for further offending. A community order preserves precisely the ties that make going straight possible.

The second reason is cost. Imprisonment is among the most expensive things a state does per head, and the money buys containment rather than the supervision, treatment and unpaid work that community sentences deliver far more cheaply.

There is a serious objection, however, which is that the public often reads a community sentence as no sentence at all, and confidence in the courts is not a trivial consideration. Some non-violent crimes — large-scale fraud, corruption by officials — cause damage on a scale that seems to demand custody whatever the physical harm involved. Sentencing has an expressive function as well as a practical one, and a system that ignored this would forfeit the public consent it depends on.

My position, then, is that community sentences should be the default for low-level non-violent offending, with imprisonment reserved for cases where the harm or the breach of trust is severe. The test ought to be the seriousness of the offence, not simply whether force was used.

Miscommunication in these areas can lead to financial loss or inadequate medical treatment. Furthermore, on a professional level, individuals often face severe career limitations, as they are frequently underemployed in low-skilled jobs despite possessing high qualifications from their home countries.

## 第699篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Some people believe that governments should place a heavy tax on foods that are high in sugar and fat in order to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Several governments have introduced levies on sugary drinks, and there are recurring proposals to extend the principle to processed foods high in fat. I agree that taxation of this kind is justified, although its value lies less in the revenue it raises than in the change it forces further up the supply chain.

The first argument is that price is the most reliable lever a government has. Public information campaigns about diet have been running for decades with modest results, whereas a change at the till is felt immediately and by everyone. Tobacco duty demonstrates the mechanism: consumption tends to fall fastest among the young and the price-sensitive, which are precisely the groups whose long-term health is most at stake.

The second argument concerns reformulation. Where a levy is banded by sugar content rather than applied at a flat rate, manufacturers have a strong commercial reason to cut sugar in order to fall into a lower band, and a number of them have done exactly that. The health gain then reaches consumers who never altered their shopping at all, which is a far larger group than those who respond to price.

The standard objection is regressiveness: a flat levy takes a larger share of a small income than of a large one. This is true, and it is why the destination of the revenue matters. Directing the proceeds to school meals, sports facilities or subsidies on fresh produce returns the money to the households that paid most of it.

In my view, therefore, the tax is defensible provided it is designed to push reformulation and its revenue is directed back towards the communities most affected. A levy that simply raises the price of an unchanged product would deserve the criticism it attracts.

## 第701篇

### 分数

Band 7.5

### 题目

Some people believe that individual efforts to live more sustainably achieve nothing while governments fail to regulate polluting industries. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

It is often argued that personal efforts to reduce one's environmental impact are futile for as long as governments allow heavy industry to pollute freely. I largely agree that regulation is the decisive factor, but I would not accept that individual behaviour therefore counts for nothing.

The case for regulation rests on scale. The emissions produced by a single household over a lifetime are trivial beside those of one industrial plant in a year, and no amount of careful recycling closes that gap. Firms also respond to costs rather than to appeals, so an unregulated company has every incentive to push the price of its pollution onto the public. Only the state can put that cost back where it belongs, through emissions limits, carbon pricing or outright prohibition, which is why the most significant environmental gains of the past century — the removal of lead from petrol, the cleaning of industrial rivers — followed legislation rather than persuasion.

The weakness of the argument is that it treats citizens and governments as separate actors. Democratic governments legislate when the political cost of inaction rises above the cost of acting, and that calculation is shaped by what voters visibly care about. A population that has already changed its own habits is far easier to regulate than one that has not, because the policy then ratifies a shift rather than imposing one. Consumer demand also moves markets ahead of the law, as the growth in demand for electric vehicles suggests.

My view, therefore, is that individual action is not a substitute for regulation but a precondition of it. Personal restraint will not solve the problem on its own, yet it builds the constituency that makes serious legislation politically survivable, and a government that fears a backlash will not legislate at all.

People across different countries are now exposed to the same styles, celebrities and online personalities, making fashion trends spread more quickly than ever before. In my opinion, this is largely a negative development because it can reduce individuality and encourage people, particularly younger generations, to seek social approval through their appearance.

People spend considerable amounts of time scrolling through applications such as TikTok and Instagram, where they are constantly exposed to international trends and influencer culture. In addition, algorithms repeatedly recommend content based on users’ previous interests, which means that similar styles are shown to them again and again. As a result, fashion trends can spread rapidly across national boundaries and become familiar to large numbers of people within a short period of time.

Another important factor is the human desire to fit in socially. Teenagers and young adults are especially vulnerable to peer pressure and are often influenced by what is considered fashionable within their social groups. For example, young people may follow viral clothing trends simply because they want to feel accepted by their peers. Consequently, they may begin to imitate the styles they see online without considering whether these trends genuinely reflect their personal tastes or identities.

When people repeatedly follow the same global trends, they may become less willing to experiment with their own style or express their personalities through clothing. Over time, this can result in greater similarity in the way people present themselves and may reduce the diversity that fashion traditionally allows. If individuals increasingly prioritise online approval over genuine self-expression, originality may become less valued.

In conclusion, global fashion has become highly influential because social media and digital technology allow trends to spread rapidly and encourage people to imitate widely accepted styles.
