## 第1164篇

### 分数

Band 8.5

### 题目

Some people think that to be successful in sports natural ability is the main important reason others think that hard work and practice is more important Discuss both views with opinion

### 文章

As with any human talent, it is often discussed what precisely turns an athlete into a successful one. Although natural ability alone may seem like the main factor, I firmly believe that training plays the most important role in sports.

Firstly, the human mind and body are very malleable. If a certain skill such as shooting a basket is frequently honed over a long period of time, one has a great chance of becoming a talented basketball player simply because their mind has adapted to perfectly perform the precise movement required to shoot the ball and score. This is true, especially from a young age: the scientific community has long delved into neuroplasticity in children and how new neural connections can be easily formed in their overly active nervous system. This serves as a powerful tool for performing well in competitive games and is the reason why the vast majority of professional athletes from the Olympics started practising in the early years of life.

On the other hand, some may feel that only innate ability could explain impressive talent and therefore is the principal requirement to being a thriving player. It is argued that congenital traits determine if one is well fit for a given sport and in the case of not having genetically acquired them, any chance of succeeding in competitions is abolished regardless of any training attempted. This is untrue because intrinsic physical advantages alone cannot magically yield any results. They are only a useful tool if put to use in a routine of constant training.

To summarize, acquiring an innate ability for sports surely provides good performance only if accompanied by persistent and hard practice. This undoubtedly elects hard work as the most important and distinguishing factor in leading a successful athletic career.

This kind of experience is meaningful and will not happen if old buildings are destroyed.

In conclusion, I do believe that old buildings have a special value. Repairing and looking after them is worth the price, hence we should not knock down the old building nor replace them with a modern one.

Spend money on roads and motorways than on public transport systems

### 文章

It is argued that more funds should be allocated to roads and motorways rather than to public shipping systems. I am in complete disagreement with this opinion.

On the one hand, I can understand why spending money on highway networks gains the support of many people. Their view is that better roadway quality would increase the levels of safety and ease traffic congestion. Firstly, the better quality of motorways means a considerable decline in route mortality and injury rates. This is justifiable since the roads in some countries are fraught with holes and obstacles, plaguing people with danger and insecurity. In this sense, the amelioration of poor street infrastructures would ensure the safety of customers. Secondly, expanding the wharf and building more motorways are believed to curb service jams. movement congestion is a major concern in big cities where massive numbers of vehicles ride on the pathway during hours of peak demand. This vexed problem could be tackled as wider roads provide maximum movement time in free-flowing travel.

However, I would argue that spending on public transport is a better investment for a few reasons. Compared to vehicles, high-capacity public travel modes can accommodate a larger number of passengers at a time. This could be exemplified by integrated and expansive public transit networks in Australia. Recent estimates indicate that each train on Sydney’s railways removes approximately 1000 cars from its wharf. Therefore, a modal shift from private to public transportation would tremendously alleviate urban congestion which has been considered as one of the productivity bottlenecks in developed economies. Moreover, efficient public transport systems are a contributor to a cleaner environment. By removing cars from streets, public transit plays a pivotal role in the abatement of carbon emissions. Not only does this reduce air pollution, but it also mitigates the effects of climate change as a whole.

Based on the above-mentioned arguments, I acquiesce in the view that money should be invested in public transport systems rather than roadway networks.

In support of this reason, a known fact is that the growing demand for products like smartphones has triggered extensive mining for rare minerals, contributing to environmental degradation. Another problematic cause is the excessive use of single-use plastics, which greatly contributes to environmental pollution. For instance, the disposal of plastic products leads to significant waste production, including non-biodegradable materials that harm the environment.

Seeing the Challenge with a brighter mind, many solutions can be helpful to curb this menace. One of the solutions is implementing laws to limit resource use and promote sustainable consumption practices. Secondly, incentivizing recycling and proper waste disposal can significantly reduce environmental pollution. Lastly, promoting alternatives to single-use plastics, such as reusable bags and containers, can further mitigate the dilemma.

In summary, the problem arises from multiple factors, including the increasing demand for consumer goods and the overreliance on disposable plastics. The primary responsibility for solving this issue rests with both governments and individuals, who must adopt more sustainable consumption habits and practices.

## 第1181篇

### 分数

Band 8.5

### 题目

The money spent by the governments on space programmes would be better spent on vital public services such as schools and hospitals. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

In recent years, governments around the world have invested heavily in astronomical missions. While these programmes may lead to technological breakthroughs and international prestige, I firmly believe that public money should be prioritised for essential sectors like schooling and medical care. These sectors have a far more immediate and meaningful impact on citizens’ well-being.

One strong reason to support the redirection of interplanetary budgets is that schools and hospitals form the foundation of any functional society. Spending billions on extraterrestrial expeditions diverts crucial funds away from basic public soft infrastructure including education and public health. Education empowers future generations with knowledge and skills and healthcare ensures a healthy population capable of contributing to the economy. Without sufficient investment in these areas, a country risks stagnation in human development. For instance, in many low-income nations, children still study in overcrowded classrooms with few qualified teachers. According to UNESCO, improving school infrastructure and teacher training can significantly increase literacy and employment outcomes. Clearly, this kind of investment delivers immediate and long-term benefits that space programmes cannot match.

Another argument is that astronomical missions rarely address the urgent needs of the general public. Even though space explorations may offer scientific knowledge, they do not solve pressing issues such as illness, poverty, or unequal access to schooling. The majority of citizens are more concerned with access to affordable healthcare and quality schooling than with planetary exploration. Prioritising these basic provisions ensures that resources are directed toward problems that affect millions of people on a daily basis. A good example is Cuba, which has invested consistently in its public health system. Despite economic limitations, the country boasts high life expectancy and low infant mortality rates—results achieved not through advanced technology, but through consistent support for medical care. Redirecting interplanetary programme budgets could allow other nations to replicate the success.

In conclusion, although astronomical missions have their intellectual and technological merits, I strongly believe that public funds are better spent on education and medical care. These foundational pillars address the core needs of society and produce immediate, measurable improvements in people’s lives. Governments should therefore prioritise the well-being of their citizens over distant, uncertain discoveries.

## 第1202篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

A small number of global streaming companies now decide which films and television series are made. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

There has never been more television, and people who worry about this concentration are usually met with that fact as though it settled the matter. It does not. What matters is not how much is commissioned but how many separate judgements decide what gets commissioned, and that number has collapsed. The development is negative for a reason the volume figures actively conceal.

Give the platforms their due first. Capital on this scale has funded work that national broadcasters could not have attempted, and distribution on this scale has done something genuinely new: a Korean drama or an Argentine thriller can now find an audience in eighty countries without a single export deal being negotiated. Writers who would once have been confined to a domestic market are watched everywhere. None of that is small, and none of it is recoverable by nostalgia for the old system.

But the old system's virtue was never its efficiency. It was that a script turned down by one commissioner could be carried to another whose instincts were different, and that unusual work survived on those disagreements. A handful of platforms measuring success by the same completion rates and the same retention curves is functionally one buyer with several logos. A project that fails their test does not fail in one place; it fails everywhere, and there is nowhere left to take it. Meanwhile a series that would once have been given a second year to find its audience is cancelled at eight episodes because a curve dipped.

That is the loss, and no count of hours produced will show it. More is being made and less is being risked. What reaches an audience has always depended on the number of people entitled to say yes, and reducing those people to a handful is a narrowing however much it fills the schedules.

## 第1203篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries, the gap between the rich and the poor is widening. Some people argue that economic growth is the best way to reduce inequality, while others believe that direct government redistribution of wealth is more effective. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Widening economic inequality has emerged as one of the defining political and social challenges of the early twenty-first century. Advocates of market-led solutions argue that aggregate growth ultimately benefits all income groups, whereas redistributionists insist that deliberate state intervention is the only reliable mechanism for narrowing the wealth gap. Having weighed both perspectives, I would argue that the evidence decisively favours redistribution as an indispensable complement to, rather than a substitute for, sustained economic growth.
The case for prioritising growth rests on the concept of a rising tide lifting all boats. When national output expands, labour markets tighten, wages increase, and the tax base broadens, providing governments with additional resources for public services. The rapid industrialisation of East Asian economies demonstrates that growth can precipitate substantial reductions in absolute poverty within a generation, and for proponents of this view, restrictive redistributive policies risk dampening the investment on which broad-based prosperity depends.
Yet this argument conflates reductions in absolute poverty with reductions in relative inequality — two fundamentally distinct objectives. Contemporary research has demonstrated that, in the absence of corrective policies, the return on capital tends to outpace economic growth, meaning wealth concentrates at the apex of the income distribution regardless of macroeconomic performance. Progressive tax structures, universal healthcare, quality public education, and well-targeted social transfers have all been shown to compress income disparities without materially impeding growth, as the consistently low inequality levels across Nordic economies illustrate.
The inescapable conclusion is that growth and redistribution are complementary, not competing, imperatives. Governments that pursue expansion while simultaneously embedding strong redistributive institutions are best positioned to achieve societies that are both prosperous and equitable.

## 第1206篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

An increasing number of students choose to complete their university degree in a foreign country rather than at home. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this trend.

### 文章

A degree taken abroad is usually discussed as though the only person with a stake in it were the student. The student's account is the easiest to balance, and it generally comes out in favour. The more interesting entries are on the other pages: the family that funds the decision, and the country that paid for the eighteen years before it.

For the student, the case is strong and mostly obvious. Some subjects are simply taught better somewhere else, and a specialism that supports three professors at home may support thirty abroad. Less obvious is what the move does to a person independently of the syllabus. Managing a bureaucracy in a second language, arriving somewhere with no existing social claim on anyone, and discovering that the assumptions you took for universal are local — these are not incidental to the education, and they are difficult to acquire while living where you have always lived.

Against that, the money is real and the distribution of it is unequal. International tuition is priced as an export, and the families who can meet it are, almost by definition, the families whose children faced the fewest obstacles already. There is also a loss that no individual chooses. A country that educates a cohort through school and then watches its strongest students take their productive years elsewhere has made a substantial public investment on someone else's behalf, and it has no mechanism for recovering it.

The honest summary is that the advantages accrue to individuals while several of the disadvantages accrue to institutions and states, which is precisely why the trend continues: nobody making the decision is paying the full cost of it. For the student who returns, or who sends money home, or who builds something that would not otherwise exist, the balance is favourable on every account at once. For the student who does not, it is favourable only on the one they are keeping.

## 第1207篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many people argue that individuals are responsible for addressing environmental problems, while others believe that governments and large corporations bear the primary responsibility. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Few questions in contemporary public discourse are as consequential — or as routinely misframed — as who should bear primary responsibility for the environmental crisis. The individual-versus-institution debate obscures a more important truth: while personal choices carry genuine moral weight, the structural levers of government policy and corporate accountability are categorically more powerful, and emphasising personal responsibility at the expense of systemic reform is not merely insufficient but counterproductive.
The case for individual action rests on aggregate logic: millions of people moderating consumption, choosing plant-based diets, or forgoing air travel could, in theory, reduce emissions meaningfully. Yet this argument overlooks the asymmetry of impact. A single legislative mandate requiring the fifty largest industrial emitters to adopt carbon-capture technology would eliminate more atmospheric carbon in a year than decades of individual recycling. The arithmetic is unambiguous.
More fundamentally, individual behaviour is itself constrained by the infrastructural and economic choices that only governments can make. Where high-frequency, affordable, electrified public transport exists, commuters switch from cars; where it does not, they cannot, regardless of environmental conviction. The same logic applies to food systems, building insulation standards, and energy tariffs. Personal responsibility is thus not independent of structural provision — it is contingent on it.
Corporate actors warrant separate emphasis. Transnational corporations externalise environmental costs as a default because competitive markets punish those who internalise them voluntarily. Only enforceable regulation can resolve this collective-action failure; no consumer boycott has ever closed a petrochemical plant.
In conclusion, framing the environmental crisis as a matter of individual virtue rather than political will and regulatory design is a category error. Governments and corporations must lead; individuals, equipped with the infrastructure and incentives that policy provides, will follow.

## 第1210篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

As countries try to reduce their carbon emissions, some argue that nuclear power must be part of the solution, while others believe that only renewable sources such as wind and solar should be developed. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Both sides of this argument want the same grid: one that emits nothing and keeps the lights on. They disagree about how long the country is allowed to take getting there, and almost every other difference between them follows from that.

The renewables-only position is strongest over a long horizon. Wind and solar are now the cheapest generation ever built, their costs continue to fall while nuclear's stubbornly rise, and storage technologies that look inadequate today have a history of improving faster than forecast. Given thirty or forty years, a grid running on renewables with sufficient storage and interconnection is entirely plausible, and it would avoid both the waste problem and the small but genuinely dreadful tail risk of a serious accident. Nothing in the anti-nuclear case is unreasonable if that is the timescale.

The trouble is that emissions have to fall now, and over the next fifteen years the arithmetic changes completely. A grid that is mostly renewable still needs something to cover a windless fortnight in January, and at present the only options are storage that does not yet exist at that scale or gas that certainly does. This is why the practical choice is rarely nuclear against renewables; it is nuclear against gas, dressed up as a debate about renewables. Countries that closed reactors in the past two decades did not replace them with wind. They replaced them with coal and gas, and their emissions rose.

That is what settles it for me, though only for a period. Existing reactors should run as long as they are safe, and a modest programme of new ones is worth the cost and the unresolved waste question as insurance against the years when storage is still too small. But this is an argument for nuclear power as a bridge, not as a destination — and a bridge is only worth building if someone is seriously constructing the far bank while you cross.

To what extent do you agree with the view that governments should intervene in citizens' health choices?

### 文章

The debate over governmental intervention in personal health choices reflects a deeper tension in liberal political philosophy between the state's duty of care for its citizens and the foundational principle of individual autonomy. Both have genuine force, and a sophisticated response requires distinguishing between the types of intervention involved rather than endorsing or rejecting government action wholesale.
The most defensible case for intervention operates at the level of commercial and environmental conditions rather than personal conduct. Food and beverage industries deploy sophisticated marketing, deliberate formulation for overconsumption, and aggressive lobbying against health-protective regulation — distortions that erode the quality of individual choice without the individual being aware of it. Governments that require transparent nutritional labelling, restrict marketing of high-calorie products to children, or levy taxes on products with demonstrated public health costs are not overriding autonomy — they are restoring the informational and structural conditions under which genuinely autonomous choices can be made.
Direct restrictions on individual consumption or lifestyle occupy quite different moral terrain. The liberal harm principle provides a coherent limiting criterion: where behaviour poses measurable risk to others — passive smoking being the paradigm case — proportionate restriction is justified. Where harm is primarily self-regarding, the calculus changes fundamentally, and paternalistic prohibition carries significant risks, including disproportionate enforcement against lower-income populations.
What the evidence consistently supports is structural redesign: default healthy options in public institutions, urban environments that enable physical activity, and sustained investment in health literacy. These approaches improve population outcomes without the coercive dimension that prohibition entails.
In conclusion, governments not only may but should intervene in the industries and environments that shape citizens' health — but the legitimacy of that intervention depends entirely on its staying upstream of individual choice.

It is argued that individuals need to be discouraged from making crucial decisions without listening to others’ opinions. Personally, I agree with this viewpoint because everyone’s knowledge is limited, and we might make irrevocable mistakes if we disregard valuable advice.

To begin with, most of us do not have a full grasp of a situation due to our insufficient understanding of the world, which leads us to biased judgements and flawed conclusions. This universal drawback, if not corrected or mitigated, may have a damaging effect on career and development, especially in terms of vital life decisions. Take the example of myself. When deciding which university to attend and what subject to study, I completely ignored all the advice and instructions given by my family members and teachers, and I ended up disliking the school and the courses I had to learn. Consequently, my life was changed by that decision that I made alone. 

Moreover, it is always beneficial to look at different ideas and discuss them with others before making a call. Doing so can not only dissolve discriminatory thoughts and prejudices but also develop the ability to think critically. The importance of listening to others can be illustrated by the famous case of Tsar Peter, one of the greatest Russian emperors and a remarkable listener. The open-minded Tsar always welcomed dissimilar opinions and even dissenting voices when he needed to modify a policy or reform Russian society. Although Peter still made several wrong choices in his long reign, his less dictatorial rule turned Russia into a formidable powerhouse in Europe. In short, as the adage “successful people are always good listeners” suggests, to reduce risks and get better results, we should avoid being autocratic and learn to be grateful for different points of view.

In closing, for the majority of us, it is injudicious to try to plumb a life-defining dilemma on our own, as it often contains complexities that are beyond our abilities. Thus, individuals need to embrace a variety of ideas before making a final decision and should not jump to conclusions without listening to others.

## 第1214篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

At many universities, live lectures are being replaced by recorded material which students watch in their own time. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

The recorded lecture is usually discussed as a loss of contact, which assumes that the lecture was contact. Mostly it was not: several hundred people in a darkened room, listening in silence to a talk that will be given again next year in almost the same words. Moving it online is a positive development, and the reason is that it removes something whose value had already gone.

What a recording adds is control over the pace. A student can stop, look up an unfamiliar term, rewind the definition and go on, which is not a convenience but a substantial difference to how much is understood. It matters most to exactly the students who look weakest in a lecture hall: those working in a second language, those without the assumed background, those who simply need the sentence twice. The traditional format offered them nothing of the kind, and its defenders rarely mention them.

The genuine cost is not the disappearance of the lecture but the disappearance of what surrounded it. Turning up meant being seen to turn up, and a student who stopped coming used to be noticeable. It also meant the questions asked in the corridor afterwards, which is where most people discover that their confusion is shared. Those things were never the lecture, but they were attached to it, and they do not survive detachment on their own.

So the change is positive if the time it releases goes into the teaching that has to be live: small groups, argument, supervision, the parts a recording cannot carry. It is negative if institutions simply bank the saving. The technology has done the useful work by separating what could be broadcast from what could not, and whether that turns out well now depends entirely on what universities choose to do with the half they kept.

## 第1215篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people believe that the introduction of artificial intelligence and automation will lead to widespread unemployment and social problems, while others argue that technology has always created more jobs than it has destroyed. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

The prospect of large-scale automation displacing human labour has generated intense commentary across economics, politics, and popular culture. Sceptics contend that artificial intelligence poses a structural threat to employment, while historical optimists point to centuries of evidence that technological revolutions ultimately expand the range and quantity of available work. I will argue that both positions contain genuine insight, but that the decisive factor determining outcomes will be the quality and speed of governmental policy intervention during the transition.
The pessimist's case draws its force from the qualitative novelty of AI. Where earlier mechanisation substituted for physical effort, advanced machine learning systems can now replicate analytical and communicative functions once considered the exclusive domain of educated professionals. This compression of the skill premium — the wage advantage that previously accrued to cognitive workers — has led labour economists to project structural, rather than merely cyclical, unemployment across sectors from legal services to medical imaging.
Conversely, the historical record provides compelling grounds for scepticism about such predictions. The anxieties surrounding early industrialisation, computing in the 1980s, and offshoring in the early 2000s all preceded net increases in employment. Each displacement created adjustment costs, yet the productivity gains from new technology consistently generated demand for novel roles that earlier forecasters had failed to anticipate. The emergence of social media management, cloud architecture, and data science as major employment categories within a single generation illustrates this generative capacity.
The weight of evidence therefore suggests cautious optimism, provided the precondition holds: that fiscal and educational institutions adapt sufficiently quickly to equip workers for roles that AI cannot readily replicate. Absent this, the gains of automation will accumulate to capital holders alone, sharpening rather than resolving economic inequality.

## 第1218篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Employers are now able to record everything their staff do on company computers. Some people believe that employers should be free to do this. Do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

The question assumes that monitoring is one thing, and it is not. A log of which files left the network and a transcript of what an employee typed to their doctor are produced by the same software and are not remotely the same act. I disagree that employers should be free to do all of it, and the reason is that the useful monitoring and the intrusive monitoring are entirely separable. Employers simply rarely bother to separate them.

Where the purpose is the system, the case is strong. A company is answerable for what leaves its network and cannot investigate a breach it has no record of, and regulated industries are required to retain communications precisely so that misconduct can be reconstructed afterwards. This kind of monitoring watches the machine, produces evidence only when something has gone wrong, and can be described to staff in a paragraph without anyone objecting to it.

Where the purpose is the person, it stops working on its own terms. Keystroke capture and screen recording are sold as productivity tools, but what they measure is the appearance of work, and anyone subject to them learns within a fortnight to produce the appearance. What the employer gains is a dataset that resembles information. What it loses is the discretion of people who have stopped exercising judgement, because judgement is not what is being counted. Surveillance of this kind does not fail because it is unfair. It fails because it is ineffective.

The test I would apply is whether an employer can say, before installing anything, what decision the data will inform. Monitoring that answers a real question, such as whether a file left or whether an instruction was given, passes it easily. Monitoring that exists because the software offered it does not, and no amount of ownership of the hardware converts that into a reason.

## 第1221篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

English has become the main language of international business, science and travel. Some people see this as a practical advantage, while others believe it threatens smaller languages and the cultures attached to them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

It is worth noticing which languages have actually disappeared over the past century, because the answer complicates the usual story. Very few were replaced by English. They were replaced by the national language of the state they happened to fall inside — by Mandarin, Spanish, Russian, Bahasa Indonesia — through school systems, broadcasting and the requirement that official business be conducted in one tongue. English is the most visible language in the world, but rarely the one doing the killing.

That the shared language is convenient is not in dispute. A Brazilian engineer and a Korean supplier can settle a specification in an afternoon rather than a month; a doctor in one country can read a trial published in another without waiting years for a translation. Whatever else globalisation has produced, this is a straightforward gain, and the alternative is not a fairer multilingualism but a slower and more expensive version of the same exchange, mediated by whoever can afford interpreters.

The danger the second view identifies is nevertheless real, though it works through incentives rather than through any prohibition. No government forbids a minority language; parents make an entirely rational calculation about their children's prospects and stop transmitting one. Within two generations a language can retreat from the kitchen to the funeral, and what goes with it is not sentimental. Systems for classifying plants, tides, weather and kinship, refined over centuries and never written down, exist only in the speech of the last generation to use them daily.

So both views are correct, but the second is aimed slightly off target. Attacking English would not save a single endangered language, because the pressure comes from the language of their own capital city, not from Washington or London. What would help is unglamorous and expensive: minority-language schooling, broadcasting and administration substantial enough that a parent choosing that language is not choosing a disadvantage for their child. English can remain the world's second language without any of this being lost — but only if someone pays for the first one.

Having a salaried job is better than being self-employed (agree/disagree)

### 文章

If one wants to work for money, there are really only two options, working for someone else for a salary and being self-employed. Most people are involved with these two options and they both have advantages and disadvantages.

Being self-employed means that the worker owns the business that is being done. This might be a small one-person business or a large company with hundreds of employees. The first advantage of this is the capacity to earn more money. If the business does very well, the income can be considerable and the owner of the company will receive the benefits. On the other hand, if business is not good, the owner’s income will be low. Self-employed people also have the benefit to some extent of choosing their working hours and holidays and they have the right to change anything within their business. With this autonomy, however, comes the pressure to succeed and the reliance on one’s employees, if there are any, to do their best to make the business thrive.

Salaried workers do not experience the same stress as the self-employed owners of companies. They might have stress in their duties, but the pressure that comes with keeping one’s own business operating successfully in order to support oneself and one’s family is just not felt by an employee. The employee also has a certain knowledge of his or her income, as the salary is usually fixed every month. The self-employed owner’s income often depends on how successful the business is. The employee’s fixed income, however, does not give much scope for earning large amounts more. In addition, an employee does not have the freedoms of the owner or the autonomy, and for many people, having control over their lives is a significant factor to their well-being.

It is certain that there are advantages and disadvantages for both being self-employed and salaried. I personally disagree that being salaried is better than being self-employed. I prefer the autonomy that being self-employed brings and, although there is more risk and pressure, this can lead to greater and more fulfilling rewards.

## 第1224篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Fraud committed over the internet has increased significantly in recent years. Why has this type of crime become so common? What can individuals do to protect themselves?

### 文章

The growth of online fraud is usually blamed on gullibility, which gets the causation backwards. What has changed is not the credulity of victims but the economics of the crime, and understanding that is what tells an individual where their own effort is worth spending.

Three things have shifted at once. The information required to impersonate somebody is now published as a matter of course, scattered across retailers, employers and social networks, so an offender begins with material that once took weeks of work to assemble. The act itself has become almost costless to attempt: a fraudulent message can be sent to a hundred thousand people for the price of nothing, which means a success rate of one in ten thousand is still a business. And enforcement has not kept pace, because a crime originating in one jurisdiction, harming somebody in a second and laundered through a third is nobody's clear responsibility, while individual losses are usually too small to trigger the effort required.

Taken together, those three facts describe a crime attempted at industrial volume against targets chosen for convenience rather than for wealth. That is the useful insight, because it means an individual is not trying to become uncrackable — only more expensive to attack than the next person on the list.

Three habits achieve most of that. Two-factor authentication converts a stolen password from a key into a useless string, which defeats the commonest attack outright. A password manager ensures that a breach at one careless retailer does not hand over an email account as well. Most importantly, treat urgency itself as the warning sign: virtually every successful fraud requires its victim to act before they think, so the discipline of ending any unexpected call or message and making contact independently, through a number you already had, removes the pressure the whole method depends on. None of these is difficult, and that is the point — the defences that work are the ones a person will still be using in a year.

Governments have limited budgets for health care. Some people believe that public money should always be spent on preventing illness rather than on treating it. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Prevention is cheaper. Almost nobody disputes it, which makes it worth asking why health ministers who announce prevention programmes go on funding hospitals. I agree that spending should tilt much further towards prevention than it currently does. I disagree with 'always', because the reason prevention keeps losing these arguments is not ignorance, and a policy built on the assumption that it is will lose them too.

The economics are not in doubt. A vaccination programme, a screening service or a serious effort to reduce smoking costs a small fraction of the treatment it displaces, and the saving compounds across a lifetime rather than arriving once. Prevention also reaches people before the point at which their illness becomes both expensive and difficult, which is the point at which a treatment-only system first hears from them at all.

What defeats it is that its beneficiaries cannot be named. Screening saves lives without anyone knowing whose; the person who did not develop the disease never learns that they were about to. Treatment, by contrast, always has a face, a ward and a family, and when a minister is asked to justify a decision it is that face which appears in the newspaper. This is not irrationality on the public's part. A society that could be argued out of treating the identifiably ill in favour of a statistical benefit would be a worse society rather than a more efficient one, and the instinct protecting them is worth keeping.

So the honest position is a strong tilt rather than an absolute. Guarantee treatment to those already ill, and route the growth in the budget towards prevention, where the marginal money does more good. The shift then happens without anybody being asked to sacrifice a named patient to an averaged one, which is the only version of this argument that has ever survived contact with a real health service.

## 第1230篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many communities, local charities and clubs are finding it increasingly difficult to recruit volunteers. Why is this happening? What could be done to encourage more people to give their time?

### 文章

Charities and clubs that struggle to recruit volunteers often conclude that people have become less willing to help. The response to any local emergency suggests otherwise. What has declined is not generosity but a particular kind of commitment — the same evening every week, indefinitely — and that is precisely the kind most local organisations are still built around.

Three changes have made that commitment harder to give. For many people, working hours are less predictable than they were: someone whose shifts are published a week in advance cannot honestly promise to run a youth club every Tuesday. People also move more often, for work or for cheaper rent, so fewer of them expect to stay anywhere long enough to put down roots, and the word-of-mouth recruitment that once filled a rota passes them by. And volunteering has acquired some of the machinery of employment — induction sessions, background checks, policies to sign — which is sensible for someone coaching children but deters someone who simply offered to help at a summer fair.

If the problem is the shape of the commitment, the remedy is to change the shape. Organisations that break roles into single sessions or short projects, bookable online like any other appointment, can draw on people whose weeks have no fixed Tuesday. Checks can be scaled to risk, so that the volunteer who serves tea at a lunch club is not vetted like the one who is left alone with a child. Employers can help at the source by granting a few days of paid volunteering leave a year. And for people who move often, a record of volunteering that travels with them, recognised by organisations in the next town, would make each move an introduction rather than a fresh start.

None of this will restore the older model, and it should not be expected to. The steady weekly volunteer, often retired, still holds many organisations together, and that loyalty deserves protecting. But a charity that can only use people able to give it the same evening every week has limited itself to a pool of helpers that is shrinking, and it has usually done so out of habit rather than necessity.

## 第1233篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many companies, software and artificial intelligence now carry out routine administrative work that was previously done by employees. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

The question of whether automating clerical work is worth it depends entirely on who is being asked. For a firm, the sum is trivially positive; for the person whose job consisted of the tasks now performed by a script, it is not a sum at all. A useful answer has to keep those two accounts separate rather than netting them off against each other.

From the employer's side the case is close to unanswerable. Work that consists of moving information from one system to another was never valuable in itself; it was the price of the information being in the wrong place. Software removes that cost, and the staff who used to pay it can be moved to the parts of the job that still need a person — the exception, the angry customer, the case the rules did not anticipate. Firms that resist this do not preserve the jobs; they lose to firms that do not resist.

The loss sits elsewhere, and it is not simply that jobs disappear. Administrative work has long been one of the few routes into secure employment for people without degrees, and what replaces it tends to demand either less skill and less pay or more credentials than the displaced worker has. Retraining schemes address the second problem on paper. In practice they are offered late, funded thinly, and aimed at whoever is easiest to reach.

So the advantages do outweigh the disadvantages, but the statement is only honest if it comes with the qualification that the two are not experienced by the same people. Where the transition is planned — notice given early, redeployment attempted before redundancy, retraining paid for rather than recommended — the balance is clearly favourable. Where it is not, a genuine social cost is being recorded as a private saving, and the arithmetic looks good only because part of the bill has been sent to someone who never agreed to pay it.

## 第1236篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries, a high proportion of young people who are released from prison commit further offences within a short period. What are the reasons for this, and how could the situation be improved?

### 文章

Debate about youth reoffending tends to organise itself around a single question — whether sentences should be tougher or more lenient — and this framing has survived decades of evidence that it is the wrong question. Reoffending rates vary far more with what happens in the weeks after release than with the length of what preceded it. The useful inquiry is therefore narrow and practical: what does a nineteen-year-old actually have on the first Monday after the gate closes behind them?

Very often the answer is nothing that would hold anyone. No fixed address, since a tenancy could not be maintained from inside. No job, because the record is disclosable and an employer with other applicants has no reason to take the risk. No qualification, because the course was interrupted and no equivalent existed in custody. What remains is the same neighbourhood and the same acquaintances, now the only people offering anything at all. Under those conditions reoffending is not a moral choice reasserting itself; it is the path of least resistance in a situation deliberately emptied of alternatives.

The interventions that follow are unremarkable and unpopular for that reason. Housing arranged before release rather than applied for after it. A training place or job held open, agreed while the person is still inside. One named worker who does not change, so that the relationship survives the transition. Limiting how long minor convictions must be declared, so that a mistake at sixteen does not foreclose employment at thirty.

The objection is that this looks like reward for offending, and it is a serious objection. But the alternative is not a harsher outcome for the offender; it is a further set of victims, and a public paying for another custodial term. Choosing between principle and results is uncomfortable. Choosing principle and getting neither is worse.

## 第1239篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries, companies are employing fewer permanent staff and are using more short-term contractors and gig workers. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Nothing about this change alters how much work needs doing, how uncertain demand is, or how often people fall ill. What it alters is who absorbs those facts. Read that way, the development is a negative one, and the flexibility it is usually defended with turns out to be a description of what happens to whoever is now holding the risk.

Employment law developed as a way of pooling ordinary uncertainty. A firm with two hundred salaried staff can carry a quiet quarter, a flu outbreak and a family emergency without any individual bearing the whole weight of them, because it is large enough to average across them. Convert those staff into contractors and the uncertainty does not disappear; it is divided into two hundred pieces and handed to the people least able to smooth it. A slow week that a company would barely notice becomes a missed rent payment for a driver.

For a minority the trade is worth taking. Specialists whose skills are scarce can price the risk they are absorbing and often come out ahead, and for people whose lives cannot accommodate fixed hours, irregular work is better than no work. But scarcity is what makes that bargain function, and most of the jobs being reclassified are jobs in which the worker is easily replaced. Without bargaining power, flexibility runs in one direction only: the platform varies the hours and the worker accepts them.

The remedy is not to abolish short-term work, which genuinely suits some people and some industries. It is to stop letting the contract label determine the protections, so that sick pay and notice attach to the work rather than to a category. Until that happens, this remains a transfer of risk from balance sheets that can carry it to households that cannot, which is a bad development however much freedom it is described as offering.

## 第1242篇

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries, fewer school leavers are choosing to study science and mathematics at a higher level. Why is this happening? What could be done to encourage more young people into these subjects?

### 文章

The retreat from science and mathematics is usually described as a failure of enthusiasm, as though teenagers had simply stopped finding the subjects interesting. The pattern looks different if you follow the incentives. Most of the students who drop physics or further mathematics do so knowing perfectly well that the work is worth doing; they drop it because the system assessing them punishes them for continuing.

Two things push in the same direction. The first is arithmetic: when a university place turns on a small number of grades, a subject with a demanding syllabus and an unforgiving mark scheme is a poor investment, and the strongest candidates are often the ones best placed to see this. The second is what happens in the classroom before that decision is ever made. A syllabus crowded with content that must be recalled leaves no room for the thing that makes science worth doing — the slow, uncertain business of testing an idea and finding out you were wrong — so the subject a student rejects at sixteen is not really the subject at all.

If those are the causes, cosmetic remedies will not touch them. Encouragement campaigns and inspirational talks address a shortage of interest that mostly does not exist. What is needed instead is to change the arithmetic and to restore the missing experience. Admissions can be made to recognise the difficulty of a paper rather than the raw grade, so that a candidate loses nothing by attempting the harder one. Assessment can reward an extended investigation alongside the written examination, which forces curriculum time to be given to laboratory and modelling work rather than borrowed from it.

Neither measure is quick and neither is free. But they have the merit of treating young people as the rational actors they are, which is more than can be said for asking them to be more enthusiastic about a choice that currently costs them.

## 第1245篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries people are having their first child at a much later age than previous generations did. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this development.

### 文章

Almost everything good about having children later happens immediately, and almost everything difficult about it happens either at the edge of biology or twenty years downstream. That asymmetry, rather than any disagreement about the facts, is what makes the development hard to evaluate.

The immediate case is strong and not really disputable. People in their thirties tend to have somewhere stable to live, an income that does not disappear if one shift is missed, and a clearer sense of what they are agreeing to. For women the calculation is sharper still, because the years in which careers are decided and the years in which fertility is highest are the same years, and an employment system that punishes absence makes waiting the rational response to a problem the individual did not create.

The costs are of two entirely different kinds. One is biological and personal: fertility falls with age, the treatments that compensate are expensive, arduous and frequently unsuccessful, and a proportion of people who intended to have two children will have one or none. This is a real loss, and it is invisible in aggregate figures because it is recorded as a choice. The other is collective and delayed. A society in which everyone postpones does not merely have its children later; it has fewer of them, and it discovers this a generation after the decisions were taken, when the working population supporting a large retired one turns out to be small.

Discussing the two sides is therefore slightly misleading, because they are not competing accounts of the same thing. The advantages are enjoyed by identifiable people now, and the disadvantages are borne partly by those same people later and partly by people not yet born. If I had to place the weight anywhere, I would put it on the observation that most of the delay is a response to insecure housing, insecure work and unaffordable childcare — which suggests the development is less a preference to be assessed than a symptom to be read.

## 第1248篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries, public confidence in politicians has fallen sharply in recent decades. What has caused this loss of trust? How might it be rebuilt?

### 文章

Distrust of politicians is often treated as a modern pathology, but it is better understood as a rational response to two changes in how democratic politics now works. Neither requires politicians to have become worse people than they were fifty years ago, which is precisely why appeals to personal integrity have failed to repair it.

The first change is that the promises have grown while the levers have shrunk. A candidate must still campaign on housing, prices and waiting lists, yet the forces that move those things — interest rates set elsewhere, supply chains, demographic pressure building for decades — are largely beyond a single administration's reach. The result is a mismatch nobody can escape: a politician who described the constraints honestly would lose to one who did not, so almost nobody does, and every term ends with a record of undelivered commitments that looks like deceit even when it is closer to arithmetic.

The second is that the record is now complete. Everything a representative says is captured, searchable and comparable with everything they said before, while the mundane work of government — a functioning department, a bill sensibly amended in committee — leaves almost no trace. Voters are therefore assembling their judgement from a sample systematically weighted towards failure.

Any serious repair has to work on those two mechanisms rather than on manners. Independent costing of manifestos before an election would make the honest candidate competitive by making the dishonest one contestable, which is the only way that incentive changes. And governments should be required to publish, annually, a plain account of which commitments they have met, missed and abandoned. Publishing failure looks like political suicide; in practice it is the cheapest credibility available, because a promise openly written off stops being evidence of bad faith and becomes evidence that somebody is keeping score.

## 第1251篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries, services that were once run by the state, such as prisons, railways and rubbish collection, are now operated by private companies under government contracts. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Whether a public service should be run by a private contractor depends less on ownership than on a practical question: can the government describe what it wants precisely enough to buy it? Where it can, contracting out is usually an improvement. The difficulty is that in many countries the practice has spread well beyond such services, and for that reason I consider the development, on balance, a negative one.

The case for it is strongest where quality is visible. A council that contracts out rubbish collection can specify the streets, the days and the standard of cleanliness, check each of them weekly, and replace a contractor that falls short. Under those conditions a private firm has every reason to find cheaper vehicles, better routes and fewer missed collections, and the public benefits from an ingenuity that a department with no competitor is seldom required to show. Cleaning, catering and routine maintenance share these features, and outsourcing them tends to work.

A prison shares none of them. What matters most there — whether inmates leave less likely to offend, whether staff can calm a confrontation before it turns violent — is hard to measure and becomes apparent only over years. A contract must therefore reward what can be counted instead, such as escapes, occupancy and cost per place, and a company paid on those terms will quite rationally deliver them while economising on everything else. Railways add a further difficulty: so few firms are capable of running one that a failing operator cannot credibly be dismissed, and a contractor that knows it cannot be replaced is under little more pressure than the ministry it succeeded. In both cases the state keeps the responsibility and gives up the control.

The development is therefore positive where a service can be specified and competed for, and negative where it cannot, and it is into the second kind that the practice has been spreading. A government that keeps prisons, and any other service whose value lies in judgement rather than measurable output, under its own management sacrifices little efficiency and retains the ability to put right what goes wrong.

## 第1254篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many countries the number of overweight children and teenagers has risen sharply in recent decades. What are the causes of this trend, and what measures could be taken to reverse it?

### 文章

Explanations of rising childhood obesity usually settle on what families do — too much fast food, too little exercise — and the remedies proposed follow accordingly: better information, more physical education, firmer parenting. The explanation is not wrong so much as incomplete, because it stops at the point where the interesting question begins. Why have the fattening options become the cheap, fast, available ones almost everywhere at once?

Two structural answers matter. The first is that highly processed food is exceptionally profitable per unit of shelf space, and profitable in proportion to how much of it people eat, which means an entire industry has a standing commercial interest in larger portions and more frequent snacking. The second is that the daily walking that once absorbed a child's surplus energy has been engineered out of ordinary life by road design, school-run traffic and the reasonable fear of letting children travel alone. Neither change was chosen by any parent, and neither can be reversed by a parent acting alone.

Solutions that acknowledge this are less appealing but more likely to work. Taxing sugar and restricting advertising to children attack the profitability directly, and the evidence from countries that have tried them suggests purchasing shifts even where attitudes do not. Rebuilding streets so that walking to school is the default, rather than a virtuous exception, restores the activity without requiring anyone to be motivated.

The honest objection is cost. Redesigning a road network is expensive and slow, and taxes on food fall hardest on the households with least to spare, which is precisely why any levy should be paired with subsidy on fresh produce rather than imposed on its own. That is a real trade-off. It is still preferable to a generation of exhortation that has already been tried and has changed almost nothing.

## 第1257篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many growing cities, most new homes are now built as flats in high-rise tower blocks rather than as individual houses with gardens. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Arguments about high-rise housing are usually arguments about particular buildings. Critics picture the neglected estates of the last century; defenders picture the well-run towers of this one. Since both describe the same building type, height alone explains very little. What separates a tower that works from one that fails is decided at street level and in the maintenance budget, and wherever both are taken seriously, the advantages of building upwards clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

The benefits of density are structural and hard to obtain otherwise. A city that expands outwards swallows farmland, lengthens every journey and spreads its population too thinly for buses, schools or local shops to pay their way. Concentrating households on one site reverses each of these at once: the bus runs frequently because enough people use it, the corner shop survives because enough people pass it, and every metre of pipe and cable serves many homes rather than a few. None of this depends on residents liking tall buildings. It follows from the arithmetic of land.

The familiar objections — isolation, crime, nowhere for children to play — are serious, but they attach to a way of building rather than to height. A tower set back from the street behind car parks and blank walls gives nobody a reason to linger at its foot, so neighbours never meet and nobody watches the entrance. Put shops, a nursery and a courtyard at its base and the same tower acquires a public life. The second failure is slower. Lifts, fire doors and heating plant shared by hundreds of households need funding for decades, and a block whose owners cannot or will not provide it becomes dangerous rather than merely shabby. A householder can mend a leaking roof; the residents of a twentieth floor cannot mend a broken lift.

The trend is therefore a good one provided cities regulate the two things developers are most tempted to neglect. Towers approved without an active ground floor, or without a maintenance fund secured before the first tenant arrives, reproduce the old estates under a new name. Built with both, they house more people, more cheaply and closer to their work than any alternative a growing city has.

## 第1260篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many large cities, ordinary working people can no longer afford to live near the places where they work. Why has this happened, and what can be done about it?

### 文章

It is tempting to explain urban housing costs by pointing at somebody: foreign buyers, landlords, speculators. The difficulty with these explanations is that the same shortage appears in cities with almost no foreign investment and in cities where landlords are tightly regulated. Something more structural is at work, and it is visible in a single comparison — cities where housing is affordable are, almost without exception, cities that have recently built a great deal of it.

The binding constraint is not money or land but permission. Over the past half-century, most desirable cities have adopted rules that fix the shape of existing neighbourhoods: height limits, minimum plot sizes, requirements to preserve the character of a street. Each rule is individually reasonable and locally popular, and collectively they make it illegal to add homes in precisely the places where people most want to live. Demand then does what it must, bidding up the price of the dwellings that already exist. The people who lose are not represented in the decision, because they are the residents a city has not yet acquired.

The remedy is correspondingly unglamorous. Permitting more housing near transport, allowing existing plots to be subdivided and shortening the approval process would let supply respond to price the way it does in almost every other market. Alongside this, direct public construction is needed for the incomes that no private market will ever serve, since a builder who must recover costs cannot house a cleaner at a rent a cleaner can pay.

None of this is painless. Neighbourhoods will change, and residents who bought expecting them not to have a genuine grievance. But a city is not a museum of its own past; it is a place where people have to be able to live within reach of their work, and that requirement has to outrank a preference for an unchanged skyline.

## 第1263篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many societies, a growing number of older people live alone and have little regular contact with others. What are the causes of this isolation, and what could be done to reduce it?

### 文章

Discussions of loneliness in old age nearly always arrive at the same culprit: families are not what they were, and adult children no longer visit. There is something in this, but it explains less than it seems to. Isolation is reported at high rates in societies with strong family obligation and frequent visiting, which suggests that whatever people are missing, a dutiful Sunday afternoon does not supply it.

What has actually disappeared is the ambient sociability of ordinary life. Most human contact is not scheduled; it accumulates through repetition in shared space — the same bus, the same counter, the same bench. Retirement removes the largest single source of this at once, and the redesign of neighbourhoods around driving has quietly removed most of the remainder. A person who once bought bread daily from someone who knew their name now receives a delivery, and the transaction that was also a conversation has become only a transaction. Nobody decided this, which is part of why it is so hard to reverse.

It follows that arranging visits, however well meant, addresses the wrong quantity. What isolated people lack is not an hour a week of intense attention but the loose, undemanding, repeated contact that makes a person feel part of somewhere. Rebuilding it means treating proximity as infrastructure: local shops and cafés that survive because planning permits them, benches and libraries and covered places to sit, and transport frequent enough that leaving the house does not require a plan.

This is slower and less satisfying than a volunteer scheme, and it cannot be announced at the end of a parliament. It also has an advantage no befriending programme can match. Contact that arises from where somebody lives does not depend on anyone remembering to provide it, and does not stop when the funding does.

## 第1266篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many towns and cities, online retailers have taken a large share of the trade that once went to shops on the high street. Do the advantages of this shift outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

The convenience of buying online is not seriously in dispute, and neither is the fact that shops are closing. What the argument usually misses is that these are not the same subject. The first is about how people acquire goods; the second is about what a town centre is for.

On the buying itself, the advantages are decisive and widely distributed. Prices are lower for a structural reason rather than a temporary one — a seller with no shopfront has costs a seller with one cannot avoid — and range is transformed for anyone outside a large city, where the alternative was never a better shop but no shop at all. Delivery is also, quietly, an accessibility measure: it reaches people whose hours, health or dependants had made an afternoon in town a serious undertaking.

The losses are real, but they are mostly not losses of shopping. Retail work was one of the last large sources of flexible local employment requiring no qualification, and the warehouse and courier jobs replacing it are neither local nor, in most cases, on comparable terms. More fundamentally, the high street was doing a second job that nobody was paying for: it was the reason people with no particular business with each other were in the same place at the same time. Shops financed that, and online retail does not.

So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages as a matter of shopping, and the interesting question is what follows from that. If the high street's value was mainly commercial, its decline is an efficiency gain and empty units are a transitional problem. If its value was mainly civic, then something has been dismantled by accident, and it will have to be paid for deliberately if it is wanted — through libraries, health centres, markets and housing rather than through a subsidy to shops that are not coming back.

## 第1269篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In many wealthy countries, a large proportion of the food that is produced is never eaten and ends up being thrown away. What problems does this cause? What measures could be taken to reduce the amount of food that is wasted?

### 文章

Food that is thrown away looks like a rubbish problem, and the obvious response is to deal with it more responsibly once it reaches the bin. But most of the damage has been done long before that point. By the time a lettuce is discarded, the land, water, fertiliser and fuel needed to grow it, chill it and move it have already been spent, and no amount of composting will recover them.

The environmental cost therefore lies mostly upstream. Farmland that produces food nobody eats is land that could have remained forest or wetland, and the emissions from growing, processing and refrigerating that food are as real as if it had been eaten. Downstream there is a further cost: food buried in landfill rots without oxygen and gives off methane, which warms the atmosphere far more intensely than carbon dioxide over the following decades. Households, meanwhile, pay for wasted food twice: once at the till and again through the local taxes that fund its disposal.

It follows that the measures worth most are those that prevent surplus food from being produced or bought in the first place. Much of that surplus is created by the way food is sold: multi-buy offers that reward buying more than a household can use, pack sizes designed for a family of four, and cosmetic standards that reject misshapen vegetables before they leave the farm. All three can be changed by regulation far more reliably than shopping habits can be changed by advice. Clearer date labelling would remove a further, entirely avoidable reason for discarding food that is still safe.

Redistribution comes next, with large retailers required to pass unsold but edible stock to food charities rather than bin it. Only after that does treatment belong: separate food-waste collection, so that what genuinely cannot be eaten becomes compost or fuel rather than methane. Each step is worth taking, but in that order. A country that invests heavily in digesters while leaving the incentives to over-buy untouched will have made its rubbish cleaner and its food system no less wasteful.

## 第1272篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In some areas, libraries, parks and community centres that were once run by paid council staff are now managed by local volunteers. Some people believe this is the best way to keep such services open, while others argue that local government should pay professionals to run them. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

When a council can no longer afford to staff a library, the real choice is seldom between volunteers and professionals. It is between volunteers and a locked door, which is why the volunteer model has spread. The question worth asking is not whether residents can run these places — plainly they sometimes can — but which residents, and where.

Those who welcome the change have a strong case. A building kept open by its neighbours is better than one boarded up, and volunteers often bring a commitment that paid staff, moved between sites by a distant department, cannot match. They know which families use the reading room after school; they raise money, organise events and treat the place as their own, because in a real sense it now is. For those who have retired, the work can also supply both purpose and company.

Those who insist on paid staff are pointing to something less visible. A library is also where people without internet access apply for jobs, where someone defeated by an official form finds help, and where a trained eye notices that a regular visitor is no longer coping. That work depends on skill and on the same person being there next week, which a rota cannot promise. More fundamentally, the capacity to volunteer is not evenly spread. It belongs disproportionately to people with time, confidence and a secure income — to the retired professional rather than the parent working two jobs — so volunteer-run services tend to flourish in prosperous districts and quietly lapse in poor ones.

That last point settles the matter for me. Public services exist partly to ensure that what a neighbourhood receives does not depend on what it can supply for itself, and wholesale reliance on volunteers reverses that principle. Volunteers should certainly be welcomed, extending opening hours and running activities no budget would cover. But responsibility for whether a library or community centre exists at all should stay with the council, and where money is short it should be spent first in the places least able to replace it with goodwill.

### 文章

The responsibility for providing funds for retirement is incredibly important and something that is often overlooked by younger people. Some believe it is the responsibility of the individual to plan for this, but others feel it is the responsibility of the state.

People who believe that the state should be responsible for funding retirees, base their argument on the fact that in most countries, people pay taxes and social charges to the government. This money, they argue, should also go towards the provision of a pension for the person paying the tax. In addition, those who have very small or no income, pay little or no tax and do not have the ability to provide for themselves. The government, therefore, in its role of caring for the population, has an obligation to pay a pension and provide other social benefits, such as medical treatment.

Many others, however, feel that it is the responsibility of individuals to fund their own retirements. As adults, they argue, people should be able to set aside and invest money throughout their lifetime, so that they can retire with few financial worries. In many countries the government has legislated a framework allowing and encouraging citizens to save up and accumulate sufficient funds for the period after their working years have ended.

I neither agree nor disagree with the statement, but rather my opinion takes in parts of both arguments. I feel that people should be responsible for saving money to fund their retirement, but I also feel that individuals who have not had the chance to do so should be supported by the government out of taxes. In my view, therefore, it is wrong to say that governments have no obligation to help people in this area. Governments are there to support the entire population of their countries, which includes the poorer elements of society.

## 第1275篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In some countries, cash is being replaced almost entirely by digital payment. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Almost every figure produced about going cashless is an average, and an average is the wrong instrument here. The convenience is spread thinly across millions of people who barely notice it. The harm is concentrated on a few thousand who lose the ability to buy things. I think the development is positive, but only in the sense that a sound policy can be handled badly, and most countries are handling this one badly.

The case for it is not in doubt. Handling notes is expensive for banks and for shops; stealing cash in quantity has largely stopped being worth the effort; a card can be cancelled in a minute and a wallet cannot. Payments that leave a record are harder to conceal from a tax authority, and the same record gives an ordinary household a picture of its own spending that it never previously had. These are real gains and they accrue to nearly everybody.

The losses accrue to people who can be named. Someone who never acquired a smartphone, or whose last bank branch within reach has closed, does not experience a cashless economy as slightly less convenient. They experience it as being unable to pay for a bus. Nor is this a transitional problem that time will solve, because the group most affected is the group least likely to change. A system can reach ninety-five per cent adoption while the remaining five per cent are simply shut out of ordinary life.

So the answer turns on whether cash is retained as an obligation rather than as a habit. A country that keeps a legal duty to accept it, and guarantees a basic account to anyone who asks, gets the benefits without abandoning anyone. A country that lets cash lapse because most people stopped using it has made a change that is positive on the spreadsheet and quietly punitive at the edges.

## 第1278篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

In some families, young children are cared for during the working day by their grandparents. Others believe that professional nurseries provide a better start. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Discussions of this question usually assume a family sitting down to weigh two options. Most are not. Nursery fees in many countries approach a second rent, and the grandparent who takes the child on Tuesday is often the reason one parent can work at all. Any honest answer has to distinguish what would be best for the child from what is actually available to the household.

Taken on its own terms, family care has real advantages that no institution can replicate. A grandparent brings a relationship that predates the arrangement, an attention ratio of one to one, and a tolerance for the slow, repetitive company small children need and paid staff can rarely sustain across a room of twelve. Continuity matters too: the same kitchen, the same walk, the same order to the afternoon. Children under three are steadied by repetition in a way that is easy to dismiss until you watch it removed.

What family care cannot manufacture is other children. Almost everything a four-year-old must learn before school involves negotiating with someone who is not obliged to give way — taking turns, losing an argument, reading a face that has stopped being friendly. Adults who love a child are, quite properly, poor at supplying this, because they concede. Trained staff add a second thing that is easy to overlook: they have seen several hundred children of the same age, so they notice at three what a devoted grandparent may not identify until five.

Weighing the two, I would place a child in a nursery for the year or two before school, precisely because affection is the one thing that can be supplied outside working hours and a peer group is not. But the argument only reaches that conclusion for families who have the choice. For everyone else the useful question is not which setting is superior; it is what a country should do about the cost that decides the matter long before any parent has an opinion.
