## 第1281篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Increasingly, people pay a monthly subscription to use products such as software, cars, furniture and even clothing, instead of buying them outright. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

A subscription is not one kind of transaction, and whether its spread is positive depends on which kind is spreading. Sometimes the fee pays for something the seller goes on providing: updates, repairs, a replacement when the model wears out. Sometimes it pays only for permission to keep using an object that has not changed since it arrived. The first is a service honestly priced; the second is rent charged on a purchase, and the recent move into furniture, appliances and features already built into cars is largely of the second kind.

Where a subscription buys a continuing service, it is often the better arrangement. Software connected to the internet has to be patched constantly, and a recurring fee ties the vendor's income to the work of keeping it safe. A family that rents a cot for the months a baby needs it, then returns it for someone else to use, spends less and discards less than one that buys. Spreading the cost also puts equipment within reach of households that could never buy it outright.

Where it merely rents out an unchanging object, the arrangement works against the customer in three ways. It costs more over any reasonable lifetime, because it is priced on how long the customer can be kept paying rather than on what the object cost to make. It transfers control: once a household's car or heating depends on a monthly payment, the seller can raise the price, withdraw a feature or rewrite the terms, and the customer's only protest is to walk away from everything already paid. And it profits partly from inattention, since a subscription forgotten is revenue collected for nothing, which is why leaving is so often made harder than joining.

I therefore regard the trend as negative, not because subscriptions are inherently bad but because their growth is concentrated where they offer least. The test is simple. If cancelling would leave customers without something the company was still providing, the fee is earned; if it would only take away what they had long since paid for, they have been leasing their own possessions. The law could hold that line by requiring that leaving be as easy as joining.

## 第1284篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

It is now common for people to change careers several times during their working lives. Why is this happening? Do you think it is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Nobody planned the end of the single-occupation career, and it is worth separating two quite different reasons for its disappearance before deciding whether to welcome it.

The first is involuntary. Automation, offshoring and the collapse of particular industries now destroy occupations faster than a working life lasts, so somebody entering the labour market at twenty can reasonably expect at least one future employer to be doing something that does not yet exist. Retraining in that situation is not an act of self-discovery; it is what happens after a redundancy notice, and calling it freedom insults the people it happens to.

The second is genuine choice, and it rests on the first. Once nobody expects a job to last, the calculation that used to keep people in unsuitable work — endure it and the pension will be there — no longer holds, and staying starts to look less prudent than moving. Cheap online qualifications made that possible in practice, allowing a second career to be prepared in the evenings rather than gambled on.

Whether the result is an improvement depends almost entirely on what surrounds it. Taken alone, mobility transfers risk from institutions to individuals: earnings drop with each restart, seniority resets, and somebody supporting a family absorbs a volatility that their employer used to carry. Taken together with portable pensions, subsidised mid-career training and a benefits system that expects periods of retraining rather than penalising them, the same mobility is straightforwardly good, because it breaks a worker's dependence on one firm and lets an economy reallocate skill without discarding the people who hold it.

My own view, then, is that this is a positive development which has been half-built. The flexibility has arrived; the institutions that would make it bearable mostly have not, and it is their absence rather than the mobility itself that people are actually complaining about.

## 第1287篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Large quantities of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans every year. What do you think are the main reasons for this, and what could be done to address the situation?

### 文章

The image of plastic in the ocean invites a tidy explanation — careless people, missing bins — and a correspondingly tidy remedy in more recycling. Both are misleading. Recycling has been promoted for four decades while the volume entering the sea has continued to rise, which suggests the mechanism producing the waste is not one that collection can outpace.

That mechanism is a price gap. Making new plastic from oil is cheaper than recovering, sorting and reprocessing the plastic already in circulation, and it is cheaper by a margin that no amount of civic enthusiasm closes. A material worth almost nothing once used will be dropped, buried or informally burned wherever collecting it costs more than it returns, and rivers do the rest. Compounding this, the countries now receiving the largest volumes of packaging are frequently those whose waste systems were built for a different, mostly organic, waste stream and were never funded to expand at the speed consumption did.

If the gap is the cause, closing it is the solution. Extended producer responsibility — obliging the company that puts packaging on the market to pay for its recovery — converts an externality into a line on a balance sheet, and firms respond to costs on balance sheets in a way they do not respond to appeals. Deposit schemes work by the same logic from the other end, giving a discarded bottle enough residual value that somebody will trouble to return it.

The objection is that these costs are ultimately passed to consumers, and they are. But they are being paid already, in fisheries, tourism and clean-up budgets, by people who had no part in the transaction. Moving that cost back to the point of sale does not create it. It simply puts it where a decision can be made about it.

### 题目

Many companies now allow their staff to work from home for most of the week. Some people think this arrangement benefits employees, while others argue that it harms teamwork and the training of younger staff. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

The argument about home working keeps stalling because the two sides are describing different employees. Those who praise it are usually thinking of someone with fifteen years of experience and a network of colleagues already in place. Those who condemn it are thinking of someone in their first job, who has neither. Both are right about the person they have in mind.

For the experienced worker the case is close to unanswerable. A daily commute takes hours that belong to nobody, produces nothing and is paid for by the employee, and the open-plan office it leads to is an environment almost perfectly designed to interrupt sustained thought. Someone who already understands the work, and who can telephone the four people whose opinions matter, loses very little by doing it at a kitchen table. What such a person needs from an office is occasional contact, not daily attendance.

The newcomer's position is the reverse, and it is the part the enthusiasts consistently underestimate. Most of what makes an employee competent is never written down: how much certainty a claim requires before you make it, which objections a particular manager will raise, when a problem is worth escalating. This is absorbed by proximity, from half-heard conversations and from watching a senior colleague hesitate over a decision. A video call transmits the agenda and loses everything around it, and nobody schedules a meeting to pass on a hesitation.

The dispute therefore dissolves once seniority is taken into account. Judged as a single policy applied to everyone, home working is neither an improvement nor a loss but a redistribution — a transfer of time and autonomy to people who have already learned their jobs, paid for by those who have not yet learned theirs. Firms that grasp this stop debating how many days a week to require and start asking which employees the requirement is for.

## 第1291篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Is using physical force to discipline children acceptable (opinion)?

### 文章

Punishing children with physical force, or corporal punishment as it is also called, is something that was accepted not so long ago and people over the age of forty may well remember it. Nowadays, however, corporal punishment is against the law in most countries and adults who practise it can be taken to court. Children are always a vulnerable group and they depend on adults for protection and education. Of course, part of the growing up process is testing and breaking boundaries and it is nearly always necessary to instill discipline on a child. Whether or not it is necessary to use physical force to do so can be a very emotive subject.

Supporters of corporal punishment often defend their standpoint by explaining that the corporal punishment is not, or should not be, excessive. They do not argue that a child should be beaten severely until he or she is bruised or cut. They argue that just the infliction of mild pain causes effective discipline and also the fear that it might be applied. People who grew up experiencing it might offer this point of view.

Those who oppose using physical force on a child would say that the vulnerability and innocence of a child means that force should never be used. Children need to trust adults and believe that no harm will come to them. Additionally, children learn from adults and it is argued that corporal punishment will only teach children that force is an answer to various problems. It is also claimed that corporal punishment has no added benefits over other forms of discipline that do not require physical force. Using it can cause psychological harm to children and should be classed as child abuse.

Personally, I do not believe that limited use of forms of corporal punishment can cause harm, and a parent who administers a mild form of it to his or her child should not be subject to criminal proceedings. Nevertheless, I would not use it myself. I can also recognise the possibilities of adults who are not a child’s parents misusing corporal punishment. Therefore, I believe that on balance physical force to discipline children should not be permitted.

## 第1292篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many countries invest heavily in training doctors, engineers and other skilled professionals, only for large numbers of them to emigrate soon after qualifying. Why does this happen, and what measures could reduce it?

### 文章

Emigration by newly qualified professionals is usually framed as a loss of loyalty, and the measures that follow from that framing — bonds, exit restrictions, appeals to patriotism — have a poor record. They fail because they treat the departure as the problem, when it is more useful to treat it as a measurement. People with portable qualifications leave when the difference between what they can do at home and what they can do elsewhere becomes large enough to outweigh everything that holds them in place, and that difference is the thing worth examining.

Pay is part of it, but not the decisive part, and this matters because pay is the part that cannot be fixed. No middle-income health service will ever match salaries in the wealthiest countries, so a strategy built on closing that gap is a strategy built on losing. The more revealing complaints concern the work itself: equipment that is missing, decisions taken by people with no clinical knowledge, promotion that follows seniority rather than ability. A surgeon who cannot operate because a sterilisation unit has been broken for months is not weighing a salary; they are watching a decade of training go to waste.

That reframing changes what is worth spending money on. Functioning equipment, adequate support staff and competent management are cheap relative to salary matching and they address the frustration that salary matching does not. Merit-based advancement costs almost nothing and removes one of the most commonly cited reasons for leaving.

There is a further and often overlooked benefit. Conditions poor enough to drive professionals abroad also drive the ones who remain out of the profession, into private practice or into administration. A country that improves those conditions is not only retaining the doctors who would have emigrated. It is retaining the far larger number who never intended to leave and were quietly giving up anyway.

If there is no financial plan for emergencies, people could be denied access to urgent healthcare needs that can help them recover. Dental treatments, for instance, could cost thousands of dollars, and the majority of people in Canada may be unable to pay the bills immediately. As a result, they would either request financial aid or resort to taking painkillers until they secure sufficient funds for the procedure.

It is indeed true that digital resources today far outstrip what can be put and stored in print books. Some people, therefore, believe that libraries with print books are no longer needed.

Another purpose that libraries serve is acting as community centres that organise events, education and childcare. Ironically, libraries also provide computers and Internet access for people who cannot afford their own.

## 第1295篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many countries spend large amounts of public money on hosting international sporting events. Some people believe that this money is wasted. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

The complaint about hosting costs is usually aimed at the wrong target. Very little of the money goes on the sport. It goes on concrete, and it is the concrete that decides whether the spending was worth anything. I agree that most host nations waste public money, but the waste is a choice they make rather than a condition of hosting.

Consider what survives. A metro extension dug to move crowds to a stadium keeps moving commuters for fifty years; a flood-defence scheme built for a riverside venue protects the district long after the flags come down. Set against that is the athletics stadium, sized for one fortnight, unusable at that size afterwards, and expensive to keep standing while a city argues about what to do with it. Both come out of the same budget and are defended in the same speeches, but only one of them is an investment. The other is a monument, and monuments are what bids are actually won with.

The reason the second kind keeps being built is that the incentives reward it. Bids are judged on ambition, the officials who commit the money are usually gone before the maintenance bills arrive, and no politician has ever cut a ribbon on a hired venue. Cities that resisted this, reusing existing grounds and putting up temporary seating that came down again afterwards, have hosted perfectly good events for a fraction of the cost. That is the clearest evidence available that the expense is discretionary.

So the money is generally wasted, and it will go on being wasted while hosting is treated as an occasion for building rather than an occasion for organising. A country with something to gain should bid. It should simply decline to leave itself a stadium it cannot fill and a maintenance bill nobody voted for.

## 第1296篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

It is the responsibility of individuals to save and provide for their own retirement. Governments have no obligation to provide this benefit. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your knowledge or experience.

### 文章

In this modern era, financial security after retirement has become the subject of considerable debate. Some people argue that individuals should be entirely responsible for accumulating sufficient savings for old age and that governments have no duty to provide pension benefits. I partially disagree with this view because personal retirement planning promotes financial independence, whereas state support is indispensable for protecting elderly citizens who are unable to save adequately.

To begin with, there are compelling reasons why individuals should assume primary responsibility for their retirement. By contributing regularly to pension funds and investment accounts, people cultivate prudent financial habits and reduce their dependence on public assistance. Moreover, personal savings enable workers to maintain a standard of living that reflects their income and long-term aspirations. For example, many employees in Canada and the United States contribute to employer-sponsored retirement plans; as a result, they accumulate substantial funds over several decades. Not only does this approach encourage self-reliance, but it also reduces pressure on government budgets. Consequently, individual saving can provide both financial security and greater autonomy in later life.

However, governments should still guarantee a basic level of support for retired citizens. While some individuals earn sufficient incomes throughout their careers, others face unemployment, chronic illness, or low-paying jobs and therefore lack the capacity to save enough. Without a public pension system, these people could experience severe financial hardship in old age. For instance, countries such as Sweden and the Netherlands provide state pensions that ensure all retirees can afford essential expenses, including housing and healthcare. In addition, this safety net narrows social inequality and preserves human dignity. For this reason, a balanced system in which personal savings are supplemented by government assistance is both equitable and sustainable.

In conclusion, although individuals ought to prepare financially for retirement, governments should not abandon their responsibility to support vulnerable older citizens. The most effective approach is one that combines personal responsibility with a publicly funded safety net, thereby ensuring financial stability and a dignified standard of living for all retirees.

## 第1298篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many developing countries have built their economies around large-scale international tourism. Do the advantages of this approach outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Whether tourism-led development pays depends almost entirely on a question the debate rarely asks: who owns the hotel? The same number of arrivals can leave a country with a middle class or with a coastline it no longer controls, and the difference is not in the tourists.

The case for the strategy is real, and it is not merely that tourism earns hard currency. It earns it in sectors where a poorer country genuinely competes. A nation cannot decide to have a semiconductor industry, but it can have a coastline, a climate and a ruin, and the capital needed to make those earn is modest by industrial standards. Tourism also employs across the whole skill range at once, which few other export sectors manage, and it builds infrastructure — airports, water treatment, roads — that residents use after the visitors have gone.

Where it goes wrong, it goes wrong through ownership. If the airline, the tour operator, the hotel and the excursion company are all foreign, a holiday can be sold, taken and paid for without much of the money touching the host economy at all; what remains is the wage bill for the lowest-paid roles and the environmental cost of the buildings. Add the exposure that comes from depending on a single sector, and a bad year abroad becomes a crisis at home.

So the advantages do outweigh the disadvantages, but only conditionally and unevenly. For a country that has legislated for local ownership, taxed the sector as an export rather than as a service, and kept some other industry alive alongside it, the arithmetic is comfortable. For one that has sold long leases on its best land and hoped, the visitors will still arrive — and most of what they spend will leave in the same week they do.

### 题目

It is widely believed that children of different levels of intelligence should be taught together, while others think that more intelligent children should be taught separately. Discuss and present your opinion.

### 文章

Whether young learners should be divided into different learning groups according to their academic grades has always been hotly debated. As some maintain that smart kids need to be grouped together, the majority, me included, believe that in providing equal resources, mixed classes may not be the most effective but the most necessary.

On one hand, by selecting the most intelligent students and reshuffling classes, these young people can get the best resources, the best materials, and more opportunities, boosting their chances of success. For example, many schools in China have been adopting this approach for decades and have produced academically remarkable students. However, the dark side is extremely unsettling. There are unhealthy and brutal competitions within these elite classes, which have resulted in unnaturally high rates of depression. Moreover, due to inadequate communication with fellow children outside of their school circles, these young ones often display stronger prejudiced attitudes towards their less intelligent peers—a disturbing phenomenon that might widen the social division. Thus, although selecting and categorising could benefit a small fraction of individuals, it is the same cohort that may suffer from the direct impacts.

On the other hand, a democratic society must ensure that each student has the same and equal access to education; otherwise, it would be a violation of basic human rights. That said, ranking young individuals by intelligence is unacceptable; depriving the opportunities of those who are considered obtuse is even worse. A mixed, diverse class that does not disproportionately allocate resources to anyone is beneficial to all. As a study suggested, students of higher levels still do equally well on exams as the ones in segregated classes, and lower-level students do better than their left-out counterparts. In other words, having students of varied abilities study together does not affect grades and could help those who are seen as unpropitious.

In summary, it is not only against modern values but also not as healthy as expected to filter children using a single-minded method—the intelligence quotient. Hence, schools should continue to create a diverse, inclusive, and felicitous environment for everyone.

## 第1301篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many major museums hold objects that were removed from other countries in the past. Some people believe these objects should be returned to their countries of origin, while others argue they are better preserved and more widely seen where they are. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Two quite different arguments are usually made for keeping these objects where they are, and they deserve very different treatment. One is that the holding museums can look after them better. The other is that a single collection which places a Benin bronze near a Greek marble and a Tang burial figure lets a visitor see something that no national museum can show. The first argument was once true and mostly is not any more; the second is untouched by anything the restitution case says.

The claim for return is not really about heritage in the sentimental sense. It is about how the objects were obtained. A great many left during military occupation or under administrations the local population had no hand in choosing, and permission granted in those circumstances is not permission. There is a plainer inequity underneath as well: a Nigerian who wants to see the work of Nigerian craftsmen needs a visa, a flight and a hotel, while a Londoner walks in free on a wet Tuesday. No argument about conservation standards answers that.

It answered it once. Fifty years ago, some claimant countries genuinely lacked climate-controlled storage and trained conservators, and museums that said so were not merely being self-serving. But several have since built institutions to full international standard, in some cases specifically to receive what they are asking for, and a defence that was empirical has quietly turned into a habit. An argument that depended on a fact must be given up when the fact changes.

That leaves the universal collection, which is the serious objection and the one I would try to preserve. It does not, however, require ownership. Long loans in both directions, jointly curated exhibitions and shared conservation would keep the comparative displays that make those museums valuable while conceding the point about acquisition. The objects should return; the idea of a collection that lets a visitor see the whole world at once is worth keeping, and there is no reason it must be kept in the same place.

## 第1303篇

### 分数

### 题目

Schoolchildren today take part in short work experience sessions instead of school (positive/negative)

### 文章

It has been a popular trend for some time now to put children into what can be called ‘work experience placements’. The children are taken out of school and take part in various types of work, usually for around a week. Some people criticise this trend, but I can’t see how it can be a negative experience.

One of the criticisms is that children lose a week of schoolwork. With the pressure to do well at school increasing, children need every bit of help to maximise their potential. Taking them out of the school, it is therefore argued, stops them from getting access to needed education for a whole week. As the students won’t really be of much help to a workplace for just one week, it would therefore be better for them to remain at school.

While this is a valid point, taking a child’s entire experience of school into account, a single week away does not make a significant difference. Indeed, if the timing of the week’s work placements is done correctly, the week can also serve as a kind of ‘holiday’ away from school, something that is regularly needed in order to allow students to remain fresh and enthusiastic. In many work placements, children also get to see some of things they learn at school put into a realistic context, allowing them to understand the relevance of what they learn and thereby creating a way to reinforce the learning.

In addition to this, schoolchildren can be quite nervous about the world of work that they will have to join at some point in their lives. By getting this short taste of what it is like, they can see that it is nothing to be scared about. As well as this, children will often have some ideas of what they want to do for a living, but are not sure. By allowing them to see a type of work they are considering, they are better able to decide whether that career could be suitable for them.

I feel, therefore, that work placements can be seen as a positive development. Missing a short amount of school is not serious and the benefits that can be gained from the placements are significant.

## 第1304篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many patients do not follow the advice they are given by their doctors. Why does this happen? What are the consequences of this behaviour?

### 文章

Patients who ignore medical advice are usually described as non-compliant, a word that locates the failure entirely in them. It is more useful to ask what the advice looked like from the receiving end, because most of the behaviour becomes intelligible as soon as you do.

Three things account for the bulk of it. The first is that the reasoning is rarely transmitted. A consultation compressed into a few minutes can deliver an instruction but not a rationale, and an instruction without a rationale has no defence against the moment the symptoms stop. Nobody abandons a course of antibiotics in defiance of the evidence; they abandon it because feeling better is concrete and the surviving bacteria are not.

The second inverts the ordinary structure of a decision: the costs of a statin or a course of chemotherapy arrive today and are felt in the body, while the benefit is a statistical event that may never happen and, if the drug works, is indistinguishable from nothing happening at all. The third applies wherever the prescription is behavioural — lose weight, stop drinking — and asks a person to sustain, alone and indefinitely, a change that their surroundings are organised against.

The consequences run outwards from there. Individually, a half-treated illness tends to return in a form that is harder to manage, so a decision that avoided a fortnight of nausea buys a week in hospital. Collectively, unfinished antibiotic courses are among the most reliable ways of breeding resistant bacteria, which shifts the cost onto people who made no decision at all. And the cheapest resource in medicine — a patient who believes what they are told — is depleted a little each time, because a doctor who expects to be ignored explains less, and advice explained badly is ignored more.

The loop closes, in other words, on the cause, which suggests that the treatable part of this problem is not the patient's discipline but the five minutes in which the reason was never given.

## 第1305篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many people believe that the current system of both teachers and students in the classroom will no longer exist by the year 2050. To what extent do you agree with this opinion?

### 文章

Predicting the demise of the traditional classroom setup by 2050 is a bold assertion, but not entirely implausible. The landscape of education has been evolving rapidly, driven by advancements in technology, changes in societal values, and shifts in pedagogical approaches.

Technology has already begun to revolutionize the way education is delivered. Online learning platforms, virtual reality simulations, and artificial intelligence-driven tutoring systems are becoming increasingly prevalent. These tools offer personalized learning experiences, catering to individual student needs and preferences, potentially rendering the one-size-fits-all model of traditional classrooms obsolete.

Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of remote learning out of necessity, showcasing the viability of virtual education. This experience may permanently alter perceptions of what constitutes a classroom, leading to a hybrid model where physical presence is no longer a prerequisite for learning.

Additionally, the role of teachers is evolving from being mere dispensers of knowledge to facilitators of learning. With information readily accessible online, teachers are shifting towards guiding students in critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration—skills essential for success in the 21st century.

However, despite these advancements, the complete extinction of traditional classrooms seems unlikely. Human connection, social interaction, and the sense of community fostered in physical learning environments remain invaluable aspects of education. Furthermore, socioeconomic disparities may hinder universal access to advanced technology, perpetuating the need for traditional classrooms in some regions.

In conclusion, while the classroom of 2050 may look vastly different from today's, with technology playing a central role and teaching methodologies evolving, the complete eradication of traditional classrooms is improbable due to the enduring importance of human interaction and accessibility concerns.

## 第1306篇

### 分数

### 题目

Should boys and girls be educated separately (opinion)?

### 文章

In many countries around the world, boys and girls are educated together. There is a group of countries, however, that educate boys and girls separately. This is frequently done on religious grounds, but not always. Having such a system can produce various advantages and disadvantages.

One of the principal reasons for educating boys and girls separately is that, if they are together, they can distract each other. After puberty, boys can be strongly attracted to girls and vice versa, and this can result in disruptive conduct in the classroom as, for example, they show off to one another. Separating boys and girls can therefore have the distinct advantage of reducing this disturbing behaviour. However, some teachers have pointed out that this model does not always work, and that separated boys and girls are equally disruptive in class, and sometimes more so. These teachers say that having the opposite sex in the classroom can actually improve behaviour.

Many educators also believe that boys and girls have different learning styles and needs. Separating boys and girls can allow teachers to address these needs more easily. There is also a belief that single sex schools allow gender stereotypes to be challenged and therefore education aspirations can be broadened.

A major disadvantage of separating boys and girls in education is that the children miss important formative behavioural development when they do not have interaction with the other gender on a regular basis. This can lead to shyness and, more seriously, dysfunctional relationships later in life. Some people also feel that mixed sex schools can promote gender stereotypes rather than reducing them.

In conclusion, I feel that children should be educated all together, although I would respect a system in which they are separated due to religious beliefs. My personal opinion is that different genders should learn to interact together from an early age, as this would allow them to develop healthy working relationships with each other.

## 第1307篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many people now decide where to go on holiday because of photographs and videos they have seen on social media. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?

### 文章

Travellers have always gone where they were told to go. Guidebooks, posters and the enthusiasm of friends steered earlier generations as firmly as a photograph on a phone steers this one, so the fact that social media influences where people travel is not in itself a cause for concern. What has changed is the kind of influence, and on balance I think the change is a negative one.

Some of its effects are plainly good. A guidebook reflected the tastes of a handful of editors; a feed reflects the experience of thousands of ordinary visitors, and it has brought custom to places that no publisher would have thought worth a chapter. A family running a guesthouse in a remote valley no longer needs an advertising budget to be found, and a traveller can see what a hostel room actually looks like rather than how its owner would like it to be imagined.

The difficulty lies in what a photograph asks of the person who sees it. A guidebook described a town and left the visitor to discover it; a striking image shows a single view, from a single angle, and invites the viewer to go and stand in the same spot. The trip becomes an errand. People queue at a particular waterfall or doorway to take a picture that already exists, and because thousands are running the same errand, a village street that once absorbed a few walkers is suddenly expected to cope with coachloads, while the rest of the region, a short drive away, sees almost none of them.

That is why the balance falls on the negative side. The informational benefits are real, but they could be had without the distortion, since reviews and maps inform travellers without telling them where to point a camera. What is lost is harder to replace: the chance of arriving somewhere without knowing in advance what it will look like, which is, for many people, the reason for going at all. A holiday chosen from a photograph tends to end with that photograph, and a traveller who comes home with only the picture they set out to collect has seen remarkably little.

## 第1310篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Many people with physical disabilities find it difficult to travel for pleasure, even within their own country. What problems do they face, and what measures could be taken to make travel easier for them?

### 文章

A journey is a chain, and for a traveller with a physical disability it is only as usable as its weakest link. A step-free train is of little value if the station at the far end has a broken lift, and an adapted hotel room is useless if no taxi at the station can carry a wheelchair. Each link is run by a different organisation that judges its own accessibility in isolation, while the traveller must pass through all of them in a single day.

The physical obstacles are the familiar part: stairs, narrow doorways, vehicles with nowhere to secure a chair. They are real, but they are also the part most often addressed, and an obstacle known in advance can at least be avoided. More damaging is uncertainty. A traveller told that a museum has no lift can go elsewhere; one told that a lift exists, who then finds it out of order, may be stranded. It is the unpredictable failure rather than the permanent barrier that persuades many disabled people not to travel at all. Behind both lies a third difficulty: when something does go wrong, nobody is answerable for the outcome, because each operator has discharged its duty on its own section.

The remedies should mirror these problems rather than simply multiply ramps. Physical access improves most cheaply when it is made a condition of renovation, since stations, hotels and vehicles are replaced continually and each replacement is an opportunity that costs little extra. Uncertainty is reduced by requiring accessibility to be described in measurements rather than symbols, checked by inspection, and backed by a duty to repair lifts within a fixed period and report their status as it changes. The absence of responsibility needs the boldest measure: an obligation that travels with the passenger, so that whichever operator breaks the chain must get the traveller onward, much as a through ticket usually entitles a passenger to a later train when a connection is missed.

None of this requires every building to be rebuilt. It requires those who run each part of a journey to answer for the whole of it, which is exactly what disabled travellers have always had to do themselves.

## 第1313篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Most people are now aware of the environmental damage caused by air travel, yet the number of flights taken each year continues to rise. Why do people keep flying? What should be done about this?

### 文章

There is no shortage of awareness about aviation and the climate; there is a shortage of reasons for any individual to act on it. That is not hypocrisy. It is what happens when the cost of a decision is spread across the entire planet while its benefit lands entirely on the person making it.

Two features of the market make flying almost irresistible. The first is that its price is fictitious. Kerosene is untaxed by international agreement, tickets are typically exempt from the sales taxes applied to nearly everything else, and the resulting fare covers the airline's costs while omitting the atmosphere's. A traveller comparing a fifty-pound flight with a ninety-pound train fare is not being wicked; they are reading a price that has had the damage deleted from it.

The second is that the alternative behaviour is invisible, including to the person performing it. Declining to fly produces nothing — no seat is removed, no aircraft is cancelled, nobody notices — while the reasons to go are vivid and personal: a grandparent on another continent, a week of sunlight after a long winter. Any argument that pits a diffuse, delayed and shared cost against a concrete, immediate and private benefit will lose, and it will keep losing however well it is made.

The remedy follows directly. If the problem is a distorted price, correct the price: tax aviation fuel as other fuels are taxed, and structure the charge so that it escalates with each flight an individual takes within a year, which places the burden on the small minority who fly repeatedly rather than on the family that goes abroad once. Then spend the proceeds making rail genuinely cheaper than flying on routes under a few hundred miles. Do that and the appeal to conscience becomes unnecessary, because the convenient choice and the responsible one finally coincide.

## 第1316篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Most people now receive their news through social media rather than through newspapers or broadcasters. Some believe this has made public debate more open, while others think it has left people less well informed. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

The two claims made about social media and the news are usually treated as opposites, but they are not answering the same question. One is about who gets to speak; the other is about what the audience ends up knowing. Both are true, and only the second determines whether the change has been good for us.

That the platforms broke a monopoly is not seriously in doubt. For most of the twentieth century a handful of editors decided what a country would discuss on any given morning, and a story without a sympathetic newsroom simply did not exist. Now a bystander with a phone can put a disputed event in front of millions before any broadcaster has confirmed it happened, and a grievance that no editor considered newsworthy can find its own audience. Anyone who has watched a national scandal begin as an unremarkable post understands what has been gained.

What has been lost is harder to see because it is not a story anyone posts. Ranking by engagement does not suppress accurate reporting; it simply lets the more arresting version of an event outrun the duller one, and corrections are almost always duller. Personalisation compounds this, not by hiding opposing arguments but by making them arrive stripped of the context that would let a reader take them seriously. The result is a peculiar kind of ignorance: an audience with more raw material in front of it than any previous generation, and less practice at deciding which of it to believe.

So the honest answer is that both descriptions hold, and that they are not equally important. Supply has improved and judgement has deteriorated, and of the two, judgement is the one that cannot be restored by adding more of it. We are better placed than ever to find out what is happening, and worse placed than we were to understand it.

## 第1319篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

News organisations sometimes publish stories that later turn out to be false. Some people believe that the law should require corrections to be given the same prominence as the original story. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

A false story and its correction are almost never read by the same people. That is the whole of the problem, and it is why leaving the size of a correction to the organisation that got it wrong has never worked. I agree that the law should require corrections to carry the prominence of the original, but prominence was only ever a proxy for something harder to legislate, and a law that fails to say so will not achieve anything.

What matters is not where a correction sits but how many of the people misled by the original ever see it. In print those were roughly the same thing: the front page reached the readership, so a front-page correction reached it again. Online they have come apart. A story can be read a million times through a search result or a shared link and then quietly amended, so that the corrected version is the only one a new reader will ever find while the million who read the false one are never told. A rule written for newsprint would be satisfied by that, and satisfied wrongly.

Drafting it properly means accepting two things publishers dislike. The correction has to be pushed to the audience that received the original, through the same alert, the same feed, the same subscribers, rather than posted somewhere that audience has no reason to look. And the threshold has to turn on harm rather than on error, because a newsroom required to give equal weight to every misspelt name will treat the rule as noise, and rules treated as noise are not obeyed.

None of this is hostile to journalism. A publication known for correcting itself loudly is more believable, not less, and the outlets that resist the idea most strongly tend to be the ones whose errors are least accidental. The obligation should fall where the damage fell: as visibly as the story, to the people who read it.

However, the idea of administering every detail of the operation on one own can be disadvantageous. ## 第1322篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

People in many countries now depend heavily on their smartphones. Why has this happened? What effects does this dependence have on individuals and on society?

### 文章

The smartphone is usually described as addictive, which places the failure squarely inside the user. The more accurate account is that it became compulsory. Two developments turned an optional device into something close to a requirement for ordinary life, and the effects that follow are consequences of that compulsion rather than of anybody's weak self-control.

The first was consolidation. The phone did not defeat the camera, the map, the diary and the bank card in separate contests; it absorbed them, so abandoning it now means abandoning all of them at once. Prices fell throughout, and networks improved to the point where the device worked everywhere, which removed the last reason anyone had to keep a substitute.

The second was institutional. Once most people carried one, organisations began to assume everyone did. Banks made the phone the second factor in proving identity, employers started issuing shifts through applications, airlines retired the printed boarding pass. Each decision was individually reasonable and collectively coercive: the technology stopped being something a person chose and became a condition of access to services they cannot opt out of.

That distinction explains the effects. At the individual level the familiar cost is attention — a device designed to be checked is checked, and the capacity for uninterrupted thought erodes without anyone ever deciding to give it up. At the level of society the cost is sharper and much less discussed. Where a service exists only through a phone, the people least able to use one are shut out of it, and a handful of firms controlling the operating systems acquire a say in who reaches a bank or a hospital appointment. A technology adopted by choice can be moderated by choice; infrastructure has to be governed, and this infrastructure was assembled long before anyone decided that was what it was.

## 第1325篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some cities have made all public transport free to use, paying for it through taxation instead of fares. Do you think this is a positive or negative development?

### 文章

Abolishing fares is one of the few transport policies that are popular before they are introduced and remain popular afterwards, and that is part of the difficulty. It tends to be judged by who travels free rather than by what the money could otherwise have bought. Judged the second way, I think free public transport is a negative development in most of the cities that have considered it, though an understandable one.

The case for it deserves to be stated fairly. Fares are regressive: a monthly pass is a trivial sum to a lawyer and a serious one to a cleaner, and for people on low incomes the price of travel can determine which jobs are within reach at all. Free travel also removes the cost of printing, selling and inspecting tickets, and in a small city where fares raise relatively little, that saving can go a long way towards paying for the policy.

The trouble is that price is seldom what keeps people off public transport. What keeps them in their cars is time, reliability and the absence of a service at the hours they need one; a free bus that comes every forty minutes is still a bus that comes every forty minutes. Removing fares therefore mostly rewards people who were already travelling, while the fare revenue that might have paid for more frequent services has gone. A city that makes transport free without enlarging its budget has, in effect, chosen a cheaper ticket over a better network, and those who depend on the network most are the ones who lose.

The social aim is right, but it can be met more precisely. Free or heavily discounted travel for people on low incomes, for students and for the elderly delivers most of the fairness at a fraction of the cost, and leaves the fares paid by everyone else to fund frequency and reach. Only where a city can afford both free travel and more services does the blanket policy make sense. Elsewhere it is a generous gesture paid for out of the quality of the very service it was meant to improve.

The debate over whether it is better to own or rent the property in which one lives is one that has strong supporters on each side. There are persuasive arguments for both points of view.

One of the main advantages of renting a property is flexibility. Usually, a tenant only has to give a month’s notice before changing where he or she lives. If a property is owned and a change is needed, the property must be put onto the market and it is frequently a long and stressful process to get a sale completed. Sometimes, the wrong time of year or a bad market can mean that a sale is not possible. Another advantage of renting is that a large amount of a family’s capital is not tied up in the property. Property can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and often a lot more. If one rents, this money can be spent on other things to help improve the family’s quality of life. If the property is on a mortgage, then the deposit, also often very large, is tied up in the property and the pressure of having to make substantial payments every month can cause a lot of stress.

Owning a property does have various advantages, though. Even though people usually have to service a mortgage every month with payments, this money is then built up with the property. With renting, the money is lost to the landlord, but at the end of the term of the mortgage, the whole property is owned by the family. This makes the process of living in a property a type of investment. In addition, the property’s value often goes up after time, frequently creating a substantial profit. Owning the property where one lives can also create a sense of well-being and self-actualisation.

The decision to whether one rents or owns the property in which one lives really boils down to individual preference. My opinion is that it is much more preferable to own a property, mainly because it creates a valuable asset for the family.

## 第1328篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some countries are considering reducing the standard working week from five days to four, with no reduction in pay. Do the advantages of this change outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

The four-day week is usually argued as though it were one policy. It is at least two. In work whose output depends on thinking, a shorter week may cost nothing at all; in work whose output depends on presence, it costs exactly one day in five. Averaging those two cases produces a number that describes neither.

Where the first applies, the case is close to overwhelming. Much of a fifth day is absorbed by the fact that it exists: meetings expand, deadlines relax, and concentration in any case does not survive four days at full stretch. Employers who have tried it in this kind of work generally report that the same amount gets done, which is less a discovery about generosity than about how little the final day was producing. The employee gains a day and the employer loses nothing, which is a rare arrangement and worth taking seriously wherever it appears.

Where output tracks hours, none of that holds. A ward covered four days a week is a ward uncovered on the fifth, and the only remedy is more staff on the same pay, which is a straightforward cost increase and a large one. Nor is the compressed alternative a solution: four twelve-hour days is a different policy wearing the same name, and the fatigue it produces cancels most of what the change was for. Small employers with no spare capacity sit in the same position as hospitals, for the same reason.

So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages across a substantial part of the economy and clearly do not across the rest, and any honest answer has to say which is which. A default of four days, with the burden on employers to demonstrate that their work genuinely requires the fifth, would capture the gains where they exist without pretending that a hospital is an office. The mistake would be to legislate a single week for both and then be surprised by the results.

## 第1331篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some governments are moving ministries and other public bodies out of the capital city to smaller towns and regions. Do the advantages of this policy outweigh the disadvantages?

### 文章

Relocating a ministry is usually judged by the number of jobs it moves, but the figure that matters is how many decisions move with them. A policy that sends a department's authority to a provincial town is a different undertaking from one that sends only its payroll processing and its call centre, and the balance of advantages and disadvantages differs accordingly.

The advantages are considerable when the move is genuine. A capital that holds most of a country's secure professional jobs drains talent from everywhere else, and a ministry of several thousand people, relocated to a town that has lost its main industry, brings not only salaries but the lawyers, caterers and contractors who serve it. Its officials, living among the people their policies affect, are less likely to design rules that make sense only in the capital. Even the capital benefits, since every office that leaves eases demand for its expensive housing and crowded trains.

The costs are equally real, but they are largely temporary. New buildings must be paid for, and many experienced staff, tied to the capital by a partner's career or a child's schooling, will not move, so the department loses knowledge that may take years to rebuild. These are one-off losses, however, whereas the concentration of opportunity in a single city is a permanent drain. The disadvantage that does not fade is the hollow move, in which the processing work is sent to the regions, the senior posts stay beside the minister, and the town receives low-paid jobs while the country's decisions continue to be made where they always were.

My verdict therefore depends on which of these a government intends. Where whole bodies move, with their leadership, their budgets and the authority to act, the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages, because the costs are paid once and the benefits accumulate. Where only the routine work leaves, the policy carries all the expense and disruption of relocation while delivering little of its purpose, and it would be better not to attempt it at all.

## 第1332篇

Band 9.0

### 题目

Research indicates that the characteristics we are born with have much more influence on our personality and development than any experiences we may have in our life. Which do you consider to be the major influence? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

### 文章

Research has established that personality and individual development are more significantly influenced by inherent characteristics than by external events encountered throughout life. While genetic predisposition undeniably plays a crucial role in shaping later developmental outcomes, it does not outweigh the influence exerted by life experiences. This essay aims to substantiate this assertion.

To begin with, one must consider the malleability of the human brain, particularly during early childhood. This developmental stage is characterized by the formation of neural connections, primarily through interactions with caregivers and peers. For instance, a child nurtured in a supportive and stimulating environment is likely to exhibit superior cognitive and social skills, in contrast to a child subjected to neglect or abuse. This phenomenon highlights the profound effect of external stimuli on development, illustrating that experiences can modify the trajectory established by genetic factors.

Furthermore, personal circumstances and social influences present compelling evidence regarding the efficacy of experiential learning. Individuals who navigate significant adversities often emerge with enhanced resilience and distinct perspectives, indicating that challenging experiences can promote growth and the development of positive personality attributes. For example, individuals who endure wars or hardships are frequently more adept at developing resilience and coping strategies in response to urgent or stressful situations—qualities that are not inherently genetic, but rather a product of the necessity to adapt to their environments.

In conclusion, although genetic predispositions provide a foundational framework for personality and development, the experiences encountered throughout one's life exert a more profound and transformative effect. The adaptability and resilience cultivated through life's challenges further emphasize the paramount importance of nurturing influences in determining individual outcomes. Consequently, it can be posited that experiences are the predominant factor in shaping our personalities and informing our developmental trajectories.

The advantages and disadvantages of high-rise apartment living

### 文章

High-rise apartment blocks are a common sight in cities around the world. They are especially popular in large cities and in locations where building land is scarce. Living in such buildings has various advantages and disadvantages for town planners and the inhabitants themselves.

The most significant advantage of high-rise apartment blocks is probably for the town planners. With land often being at a premium in large cities, one way to maximise space is to build upwards, so that the population density per square kilometre can be increased. The demand for housing in big cities can therefore be more easily met. There are also disadvantages for town planners. The heavier population density can put added pressure on social facilities, for example sewage and other waste disposal, and the provision of adequate school and medical services.

There are also advantages and disadvantages for the actual inhabitants of high-rise apartment blocks. With the demand for housing being reduced, prices are therefore not as high, making housing more affordable. Many people also like not having to be responsible for a garden, and living in an apartment has this advantage. Finally, with so many people living in the same area, many friendships can be made and a community spirit can be built up. It appears the most significant disadvantage is that, in practice, living in high-rise apartment blocks is just not the lifestyle many people want. In some city neighbourhoods, these living spaces can often be associated with poor living conditions and undesirable social elements. In addition, many people view high-rise apartment blocks as being unsafe. For example, in the case of fire, tall buildings are difficult or impossible to evacuate safely.

It is clear that high-rise apartment blocks have benefits and drawbacks. It is also clear, however, that due to the need to house increasing numbers of people in cities, these architectural features are here to stay, whether people like them or not.

## 第1334篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some governments now fund university places only in subjects that lead directly to employment. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Higher education is expensive, and the money that pays for it has to come from somewhere, so it is not unreasonable for a government to ask what its subsidy buys. My objection is not to the question but to the answer most funding formulas give, which treats a graduate's first salary as though it settled the matter.

Where a shortage is real and documented, targeted funding is straightforward good policy. A health service short of radiographers cannot conjure them out of a general commitment to learning; it needs places, in named programmes, paid for now against a need that will bite in five years. Steering money towards those places is not an attack on scholarship but the ordinary business of planning, and the alternative — subsidising every application equally and hoping the aggregate comes out right — has left some fields with graduate surpluses and others with chronic vacancies.

The trouble begins when employability stops being one input among several and becomes the only one. Earnings measured three years after graduation describe the labour market of the year a particular cohort happened to leave university, and they describe it only for the jobs that existed then. They cannot register the teacher a philosophy graduate becomes at forty, and they could not have anticipated that several of today's safest industries would be built on research that looked unusable a generation ago. Nor do they price what a country forfeits when the last people able to read its own archives are hobbyists.

So I would keep the shortage-driven funding and abandon the salary league tables that increasingly accompany it. Direct money where the evidence of need is specific; protect a floor beneath the disciplines whose payoff is diffuse and slow; and accept that some of what a university produces will never appear on a return-on-investment statement — which is an argument for funding it publicly, not an argument against funding it at all.

The majority of former prisoners commit further crime after their release (reasons and solutions)

### 文章

It is a sad fact that criminals who leave prison go on to commit further crime. There are various reasons for this, but there are also some things that can be done to prevent it from happening.

One reason for this recidivism is due to a lack of legitimate income. Many people turn to crime as they cannot find an alternative to earn money. When such person comes out of prison, it is very often the case that they have the same few opportunities for a legitimate income. In fact, these opportunities will even be reduced, as employers are often less willing to give an ex-prisoner a job. Some people also return to crime, as they spend all the time of their prison sentence with other criminals. This is not a great environment for rehabilitation, and sometimes even a network of contacts can be made to help develop criminal activities on release.

One important way to help address this problem is education. Criminals who have turned to illegal activities because of no alternatives to earn a living need to learn a way to earn a wage, such as a trade or vocational skills. Computer skills, for example, are in high demand and someone trained in these could very possibly find work. In addition, governments can offer incentives to employers to attract them to give jobs to newly-released prisoners. This would help people who don’t really want to return to crime achieve a fresh start. As keeping people in prison is an expensive business, governments might find it cheaper to pay these incentives.

To sum up, people returning to crime is a tragedy that should be avoided if at all possible in today’s society. Education and incentives can directly address the reasons for it and could make society a happier and safer place.

## 第1337篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people argue that offenders who have committed non-violent crimes should serve their sentences in the community rather than in prison. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

The distinction the question draws is doing more work than it can bear, so I would support the reform while rejecting the line it has been drawn on. What determines whether custody helps is not whether force was used but whether the sentence has anything to accomplish that liberty would prevent.

For most low-level acquisitive offending it does not. Three months removes a person from a job they will not get back, a tenancy that will not be held open and a family that absorbs the cost of their absence, and returns them with a criminal record and a weakened set of reasons to stay out of trouble. Nothing in those three months touches the addiction, the debt or the chaotic housing that produced the offence, because nothing worth starting can be finished in twelve weeks. The sentence is not too harsh or too soft. It is the wrong tool, and its main measurable achievement is to make the next offence more likely than it was.

Community disposals can be the right tool, but only where they are actually resourced. An unpaid work requirement with no treatment attached, supervised by a probation officer carrying eighty other cases, is not a sentence, and the public is right to notice. This is where the argument is usually lost — not on principle, but because underfunded alternatives fail visibly and prison then looks like the responsible choice.

Where I part from the proposal is over its category. A fraud that empties a pension scheme is non-violent, and there is no serious case for a community order: the harm is enormous, the offender is rarely chaotic, and deterrence in that population responds to precisely one thing. A scuffle outside a pub, meanwhile, is violent and may well be better answered outside prison.

So the reform is right and its criterion is wrong. Sentence according to the harm done and to what a sentence can realistically achieve, rather than according to whether anybody was hit.

### 题目

Should a city try to preserve its old, historic buildings or destroy them and replace them with modern buildings? Use specific reasons and examples to support your opinion.

### 文章

Whether cities should preserve historic buildings or demolish them to make space for modern developments is a topic of considerable debate. I strongly believe that maintaining old structures is far more beneficial, as they carry cultural value and can bring long-term economic advantages.

One major reason to preserve historic buildings is that they represent a city’s cultural identity. These structures reflect architectural styles, traditions and significant events from different periods of history. When cities destroy them, they risk losing part of their heritage that cannot be replaced. For example, many European cities, such as Rome and Prague, attract millions of visitors every year precisely because they have maintained their historic centres. These buildings create a unique atmosphere that modern skyscrapers cannot replicate. Therefore, preserving old architecture helps maintain a sense of continuity and identity for future generations.

Another strong argument for preservation is the economic value that historic sites generate. Tourism is one of the largest global industries, and travellers often choose destinations based on their cultural and historical attractions. Renovating old buildings and converting them into museums, hotels or cultural centres not only protects heritage but also supports local businesses and creates employment. Additionally, many historic buildings are structurally sound and can be modernised internally, making them both functional and environmentally sustainable. In contrast, demolishing structures and constructing new ones often requires far more energy and resources, contributing to environmental waste.

In conclusion, cities should prioritise the preservation of historic buildings because they provide cultural identity and long-term economic benefits. While modern development is important, it should not come at the expense of irreplaceable heritage that enriches both local residents and visitors.

## 第1340篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people believe that governments should place a heavy tax on foods that are high in sugar and fat in order to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Behind this question sits an assumption worth examining: that the problem is what people choose, and that a tax works by making them choose differently. Read that way the levy is a blunt instrument, mildly punitive and easy to resent. I support it, but for a reason that has very little to do with the shopper at the checkout.

Diets did not deteriorate because whole populations lost their willpower simultaneously. They deteriorated because the cheapest, most available and most heavily marketed calories were reformulated over half a century to be as close to irresistible as food engineering could make them. Asking individuals to out-compete that through discipline alone is a strategy with an unbroken record of failure, and the moralising that accompanies it does real damage to the people it targets.

A tax banded by composition changes the incentive at the point where the decisions are actually taken. A manufacturer facing a threshold will quietly take sugar out of a recipe rather than surrender a price advantage, and consumers who never read a label and never intended to change anything consume less sugar. That is the entire case, and it is a strong one: it operates on the environment rather than the individual, so it requires nobody to be persuaded of anything.

Two conditions follow. The levy has to be graded rather than flat, since a flat charge gives no reason to reformulate and merely raises the price of an unchanged product. And it has to be paired with supply — fresh food that is genuinely cheaper and genuinely nearby — or it becomes a charge on people whose alternatives are theoretical. Without both, the criticism that it punishes poverty is not a smear; it is accurate.

So I agree with the proposal, with the caveat that its purpose is routinely misdescribed. Taxes of this sort do not work by shaming. They work by making the reformulated version the commercially obvious one, which is why the healthiest possible outcome is a tax that eventually collects almost nothing.

## 第1343篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people believe that individual efforts to live more sustainably achieve nothing while governments fail to regulate polluting industries. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

The claim contains a truth worth separating from the conclusion drawn out of it. No household's recycling will offset a coal plant, and anyone who believes otherwise has misread the arithmetic badly. What does not follow is that personal behaviour is pointless, because the question was never whether individual action solves the problem; it is what individual action is for.

Regulation does the actual work here, and the confusion has been convenient for the industries that would rather be lectured than legislated against. It is no accident that the language of personal footprints has been promoted most enthusiastically by the companies with the largest ones. A citizen who spends a decade of political energy on shorter showers has been, in the most literal sense, diverted.

But that argument proves too much. Habits are not only emissions; they are evidence of what a population will tolerate. Every government that has priced carbon and kept the policy in place did so in a society where the behaviour was already spreading, so that the law ratified a change rather than initiating one. Where that groundwork is missing, ambitious policy tends to survive until the first fuel protest or the next election. Personal action is a poor lever on emissions and an unusually good one on political feasibility, and treating those as the same lever is what makes this debate circular.

So I disagree with the claim while accepting its premise. Live more sustainably by all means, but keep the two purposes apart. The recycling is close to worthless as mitigation and genuinely useful as a signal, while an hour spent on a council planning objection or a pension fund's holdings is worth more than either. The error is not caring about personal conduct; it is letting personal conduct feel like the whole of the obligation, which is precisely the outcome the polluters would choose if they were choosing.

## 第1346篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people believe that newspapers and websites should be free to publish stories about the private lives of famous people. Others think that famous people have the same right to privacy as anyone else. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

### 文章

Both sides of this argument treat fame as the deciding factor: one holds that celebrity is a bargain in which privacy is the price, the other that a famous person remains a person. Each captures something true, but fame seems to me the wrong test. Whether a private fact may be published should depend on whether it bears on a role its subject holds in public, and on that basis many famous people deserve more protection than they receive, while some obscure ones deserve less.

The case for freedom to publish is strongest where power is involved. A minister who conceals a financial interest in a company his department regulates, or a magistrate whose private dealings call her impartiality into question, has a private life that is also a public matter, and a press forbidden to report it would be failing in its most important function. The bargain argument has some force too. A celebrity who sells magazines an idealised picture of family life, and earns endorsements from it, can hardly object when the picture is exposed as false, because the falsehood was part of what was sold.

The case for privacy is strongest everywhere else, which is to say in most of what is actually published. An actor's illness, a footballer's divorce and photographs of a singer's children on the way to school inform the public of nothing that affects it; they are interesting to the public rather than in the public interest, and the distinction is not a technicality. The person pursued pays in anxiety, strained relationships and the loss of any ordinary life, and relatives who never chose publicity pay alongside them.

My own view, then, is that neither position should be accepted whole. Public figures surrender privacy only in the areas their public role touches: a politician's finances, a campaigner's consistency with the cause they promote, a celebrity's honesty about whatever they have chosen to sell. Beyond those areas fame confers no licence to intrude, and a rule built on that principle would protect most famous people while leaving the press free to do the reporting that genuinely matters.

## 第1349篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people believe that private cars should be banned from the centres of large cities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Bans are rarely the interesting part of a transport policy, and treating this as a question about cars obscures what is actually being decided. A city centre is a fixed quantity of land. Every decision about vehicles is a decision about how that land is divided, and the private car is simply the most expensive user of it per person moved.

Seen that way the case is straightforward. A lane of traffic and the parking that serves it consume a strip of the most valuable ground in the country in order to move a few hundred people an hour; the same strip carries many times that number as a bus lane, a cycle track or a pavement. Nothing in that arithmetic depends on disliking motorists. It is why districts that reallocate the space almost always end up busier than before, and why the retailers who campaign hardest against pedestrianisation are so often the ones who benefit from it.

The objection that matters is not about congestion or trade but about who gets left behind. For a wheelchair user, a plumber with a van, or a cleaner finishing a shift at two in the morning, a car is not a lifestyle choice, and a ban presented as a moral correction of selfish behaviour will fall hardest on people whose behaviour was never the problem. Any scheme worth supporting begins with blue badges, loading windows and a night bus that actually runs.

Sequence matters just as much. Restrict driving before the alternatives exist and the policy fails on its own terms, generating a resentment that outlives the administration which introduced it. Build the tram first and the traffic thins before anyone has been compelled to do anything.

So I agree, with the emphasis moved. The aim is not to punish drivers but to stop allocating the scarcest public land to the least efficient possible use of it — and done in that order, the ban is less a prohibition than a formality confirming a change most people have already made.

## 第1352篇

### 分数

Band 9.0

### 题目

Some people believe that voting in national elections should be compulsory for all adult citizens. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

### 文章

Compulsory voting is usually argued about as though the disagreement were between people who value participation and people who value liberty. It is not. Almost everyone involved wants a legitimate government chosen by a representative electorate; what they disagree about is whether a law can produce one.

The case for compulsion is stronger than its opponents tend to concede. Voluntary turnout is not random. It correlates closely with age, income and education, so a voluntary electorate is a systematically distorted sample of the population, and parties respond rationally by writing manifestos for the people who show up. Pensioners are courted and renters are not, and the asymmetry compounds over decades into a settlement nobody ever voted for as such. Compulsion corrects the sample, and no amount of enthusiasm for liberty makes that correction unnecessary.

What it cannot correct is the reason people stay away. Non-voting in mature democracies is concentrated among citizens who have concluded, often accurately, that their vote will not change anything where they live. Requiring them to attend converts a withdrawal of consent into a mark on a ballot paper, and the government that results can claim a mandate it has not earned. That is not a minor cost. It removes the only signal the disaffected currently possess, and it removes it precisely when it has become loudest.

There is a version of the policy I would accept. If the legal duty is to attend rather than to endorse, and the ballot carries a formal option to support none of the candidates, the compulsion falls on the state to present itself to every citizen instead of on the citizen to approve of what is presented. Turnout figures then become informative rather than decorative, and abstention survives as something countable.

So I disagree with compulsory voting as it is normally proposed, and would support it in that amended form. Making people vote is, in the end, a way of not asking why they stopped.
